add_subtopics.title: User provisioning and deprovisioning: JIT and SCIM
add_subtopics.body:
SSO proves who a user is, but your app still needs a user record, roles and, just as important, a way to remove access. There are two common ways to create users.

Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning creates the user the first time they log in through SSO. It is easy: read email, name and groups from the ID token or SAML assertion and insert a row. The weakness is offboarding. When someone leaves, the IdP disables them, but your app never hears about it. Their row stays active, any long-lived API key keeps working, and a group change only reaches you at their next login.

SCIM 2.0 (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) fixes that. The IdP (Okta, Entra ID, OneLogin) pushes changes to your app over a small REST API: POST /scim/v2/Users to create, PATCH to update, PATCH with active set to false (or DELETE) to deactivate, and /scim/v2/Groups to sync group membership. The customer's IT team configures it once, with a base URL and a bearer token you give them. From then on, joiners, movers and leavers flow automatically.

Deprovisioning is what security reviewers test. When a user is deactivated, your app must end their sessions, revoke their refresh tokens and API keys, and keep their data and audit history (do not hard-delete records other people rely on). Each IdP formats PATCH requests a little differently, so test with the IdP's own SCIM test tool and log every SCIM call.
add_subtopics.example: Fernhollow Surveys, a 3,000-person firm, pilots your app with JIT users. In the security review they ask: 'If we fire someone at 5 pm, when do they lose access?' With JIT the honest answer is 'at the next token refresh, and API keys never'. You add SCIM: IT points Okta at https://app.example.com/scim/v2 with a token, and a test deactivation of a pilot user ends her sessions within a minute. The review item is closed.

add_subtopics.title: Enterprise identity plumbing: groups, roles and mTLS
add_subtopics.body:
Big customers manage access in Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) or Active Directory groups, and they expect your app to follow those groups. There are two ways to receive them.

Group claims send the user's groups inside the token. Entra sends group object ids (GUIDs such as 4f1c2a7e-...), not readable names, so you keep a mapping table from id to your role, agreed in writing with IT. Watch for group overage: if a user is in too many groups (more than 200 in a JWT), Entra leaves the groups out and adds a pointer telling you to ask Microsoft Graph instead. Code that treats a missing list as 'no groups' silently locks those users out, or worse, grants a default role.

App roles are often cleaner. The customer defines roles such as Claims.Approver on your app registration in Entra and assigns groups to them, and the token then carries a roles claim with those names. No GUID table is needed on your side.

Inside the network, services also need to prove who they are to each other. mTLS (mutual TLS) means both sides present certificates during the TLS handshake, not only the server. The pricing service accepts a call only if the client certificate was signed by the internal CA and names an allowed service. In Kubernetes a service mesh such as Istio or Linkerd does this automatically for every pod. Without a mesh, you load a client certificate and key in your HTTP client, as in the code, and rotate them before they expire.
add_subtopics.example: A bank's IT team sends a spreadsheet: group FraudOps-Analysts (object id 4f1c...) should be adjuster, and group FraudOps-Readonly should be viewer. You load it into GROUP_TO_ROLE, and a test user who belongs to 250 groups triggers the overage path, which you handle with a Graph call. Their platform team also requires mTLS between your API and their pricing service, so they issue you a client certificate from their internal CA.

add_subtopics.title: OWASP Top 10 2025 and SSRF defences that hold
add_subtopics.body:
OWASP updated its Top 10 in 2025, and security reviewers are starting to cite the new numbering. Two changes matter for FDEs. Software supply chain failures is now its own item (A03): vulnerable or compromised dependencies, build tools and CI pipelines, not just 'outdated components'. And SSRF (server-side request forgery) is no longer a separate entry: it is folded into A01 Broken access control, which is still number one. For apps built on LLMs there is a separate list, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, which starts with prompt injection; the guardrails topic covers it.

The earlier SSRF advice (allowlist hosts, block private addresses) has two gaps that testers love. First, redirects: the allowed host answers with a 302 to http://169.254.169.254/, and an HTTP client that follows redirects fetches the metadata service. Turn off automatic redirects and check every hop yourself. Second, DNS rebinding: the attacker's domain resolves to a public IP when you check it and to 10.0.0.7 a second later when you connect. Resolve the name yourself, check every returned IP, and connect to the IP you checked, or send all outbound fetches through an egress proxy that enforces the block list at connect time. In the cloud, also require IMDSv2 on AWS so the metadata service needs a session token.
add_subtopics.example: A pen tester at Fernhollow Surveys reports that your 'summarize this link' tool can read cloud credentials. Their URL was on an allowed domain, but it redirected to 169.254.169.254. You switch off automatic redirects, re-check each hop and pin the checked IP. The retest shows every internal target blocked.

replace_subtopics.title: Authentication versus authorization
replace_subtopics.body:
Authentication proves identity. Common factors are something you know (a password), something you have (a phone app or hardware key) and something you are (a fingerprint). Using two or more is multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Authorization happens after authentication. It checks a rule: may this user do this action on this thing? The rule lives in your code or a policy engine, and it must run on the server for every request.

HTTP gives each failure its own status code. 401 Unauthorized really means 'not authenticated, please log in'. 403 Forbidden means 'I know who you are, and you may not do this'.

If your app owns the passwords (no IdP), never store them as plain text or as a fast hash such as SHA-256. A fast hash lets an attacker who steals the table test billions of guesses per second. Use a slow, salted password hash made for the job: argon2id (the current first choice) or bcrypt. The library adds a random salt, so two users with the same password get different hashes.

MFA factors are not equally strong. From weakest to strongest: SMS codes (can be stolen by SIM swap), TOTP codes from an authenticator app (can still be typed into a fake login page), push approval (users can be tricked into tapping Approve, so prefer push with number matching), and passkeys or hardware keys that use WebAuthn. A passkey is phishing resistant: the browser only releases the signature to the real website domain, so a look-alike site gets nothing. When a customer asks for "strong MFA", they usually mean passkeys, FIDO2 keys or push with number matching.
replace_subtopics.example: Priya, an analyst at Harlow Mutual Insurance, logs in with her password and an Okta Verify push. She is authenticated. She opens the claims dashboard and it loads, because analysts may read claims. She clicks 'Approve payout' and gets a 403, because only the adjuster role may approve. If her session had expired she would have received a 401 and been sent back to log in. The customer's security team also asks how local admin accounts are protected. You answer: passwords hashed with argon2id, and MFA through passkeys, with SMS disabled.

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()

def current_user(token: str = Depends(read_bearer_token)):
    user = verify_token(token)           # AuthN: who is this?
    if user is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Please log in")

    if "adjuster" not in user.roles:     # AuthZ: may they do it?

from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError

print(ph.verify(stored, "correct horse battery"))  # True

replace_subtopics.title: Sessions versus tokens
replace_subtopics.body:
After login the server must remember you on the next request, because HTTP itself forgets everything between requests. There are two common ways.

A session stores the login state on the server (in memory, Redis or a database) and gives the browser a random session id in a cookie. Every request sends the cookie and the server looks the id up. Logging someone out is easy: delete the row.

A token puts the facts into the credential itself. The most common kind is a JWT (JSON Web Token): three base64 parts, a header, a payload of claims (user id, expiry, roles) and a signature. Any server holding the right key can verify it without a lookup, which suits APIs and many services. The cost is that a token stays valid until it expires, so access tokens are kept short (minutes to an hour) and refreshed with a separate refresh token.

Cookie flags matter as much as the cookie. HttpOnly stops page JavaScript from reading it, so an XSS bug cannot copy the session. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite controls whether the browser attaches it to requests started by another website. That matters because of CSRF (cross-site request forgery): a malicious page makes your browser submit a form to your bank, and the browser helpfully adds your bank cookie. SameSite=Lax (or Strict) stops the cookie riding along on those cross-site POSTs, and an anti-CSRF token (a random value the server puts in its own forms and checks on submit) stops the rest. A single-page app should not keep tokens in localStorage, because any injected script can read localStorage; keep them in HttpOnly cookies or let a small backend (a BFF, backend for frontend) hold them.

Refresh tokens need care too. Use rotation: every refresh returns a new refresh token and the old one stops working. If an old one is ever presented again, someone copied it, so revoke the whole login. To force-logout a JWT user before expiry, keep access tokens short (5 to 15 minutes), revoke their refresh token, and for urgent cases check a small deny-list of token ids (the jti claim) on every request.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer's web app uses a session cookie for store managers in the browser. Its mobile app and partner integrations call the same backend with JWT access tokens that expire after 15 minutes. When a manager leaves the company, IT disables them in Entra ID: the web session is deleted at once, and the mobile app fails at its next refresh because the IdP refuses to issue new tokens. When the retailer's security team asks 'how do you log out a stolen phone within minutes?', the answer is: revoke that login's refresh tokens, put the current access token's jti on the deny-list, and the 15-minute expiry covers the rest.

import jwt, time   # PyJWT

SECRET = load_from_vault("jwt-signing-key")   # never hard-code

token = jwt.encode(
    {"sub": "user-812", "roles": ["analyst"],
     "exp": int(time.time()) + 900},          # expires in 15 min
    SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

claims = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])  # checks sig + exp
print(claims["sub"], claims["roles"])
# The payload is only base64: anyone can read it. Never put secrets inside.

# --- Cookie flags, refresh rotation and forced logout ---
# Cookie flags for a browser session (FastAPI)
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
import secrets

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/login")
def login(response: Response):
    response.set_cookie(
        "session_id", secrets.token_urlsafe(32),
        httponly=True,     # page JavaScript cannot read it (limits XSS theft)
        secure=True,       # only sent over HTTPS
        samesite="lax",    # not sent on POSTs started by other sites (blocks CSRF)
        max_age=8 * 3600)  # 8 hours
    return {"ok": True}

cookie = TestClient(app).post("/login").headers["set-cookie"]
print(cookie.split(";", 1)[1].strip())
# HttpOnly; Max-Age=28800; Path=/; SameSite=lax; Secure

# Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, plus a deny-list for access tokens
refresh_store = {}      # refresh token -> {"user", "family", "used"}
denied_jti = set()      # ids (jti) of access tokens we force-logged-out

def issue(user, family=None):
    family = family or secrets.token_hex(4)          # one family per login
    rt = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)
    refresh_store[rt] = {"user": user, "family": family, "used": False}
    return rt

def refresh(rt):
    rec = refresh_store.get(rt)
    if rec is None:
        return "unknown token"
    if rec["used"]:                                   # an old token came back: stolen
        for r in refresh_store.values():
            if r["family"] == rec["family"]:
                r["used"] = True                      # kill the whole login
        return "reuse detected: login revoked"
    rec["used"] = True                                # each refresh token works once
    return issue(rec["user"], rec["family"])

first = issue("user-812")
second = refresh(first)             # normal rotation: a new token
print(refresh(first))               # reuse detected: login revoked
print(refresh(second))              # reuse detected: login revoked

def access_allowed(claims):
    return claims["jti"] not in denied_jti            # checked on every request

denied_jti.add("a1b2")              # admin clicks "force logout"
print(access_allowed({"sub": "user-812", "jti": "a1b2"}))   # False

replace_subtopics.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
replace_subtopics.body:
OAuth 2.0 is a standard for delegated access: an app gets an access token that lets it call an API on a user's behalf without ever seeing their password. The part that issues tokens is the authorization server. Scopes limit what the token may do, such as read:calendar.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds identity. Along with the access token, you receive an ID token, a JWT that says who logged in (sub, email, name) and which IdP vouched for them (iss).

The authorization code flow is the one to use for web apps. The browser only ever carries a short one-time code, and your server swaps it for tokens over a direct back-channel call. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) adds a random secret created per login, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed by anyone else. The state parameter ties the callback to the login this browser started, which blocks forged callbacks.

Tokens from an IdP are normally signed with RS256: the IdP signs with a private key and publishes the matching public keys at a JWKS URL (JSON Web Key Set, listed in the discovery document as jwks_uri). Each token header has a kid (key id) that says which key signed it. Your app fetches the JWKS, picks the key with that kid, and verifies the signature. IdPs rotate keys, so cache the JWKS and refetch when an unknown kid appears. You never share a secret with the IdP for this, unlike the HS256 example in the previous subtopic.

Always pin the algorithm you expect, for example algorithms=["RS256"]. Old libraries trusted the alg field inside the token, which allowed two attacks: alg=none (a token with no signature at all) and algorithm confusion (switching to HS256 and using the public key as the secret). Also check iss (issuer), aud (your client id) and exp every time.
replace_subtopics.example: A logistics company wants its dispatchers to log in to your route-planning app with Okta. You register an OIDC app in their Okta tenant with redirect URI https://routes.example.com/callback and receive a client id and secret. Your app reads Okta's discovery document, redirects to the authorize endpoint, and on callback verifies the ID token's issuer, audience and expiry before creating a session. In the logistics pilot, your callback handler verifies the ID token against Okta's JWKS with algorithms pinned to RS256. When Okta rotates its signing key three months later, the new kid triggers one refetch and nobody notices.

# The authorize redirect (one line, split for reading)
GET https://keelridge.okta.com/oauth2/default/v1/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=0oa1routes
  &redirect_uri=https://routes.example.com/callback
  &scope=openid%20email%20profile%20groups
  &state=Xy7...random
  &code_challenge=E9Mel...sha256-of-verifier
  &code_challenge_method=S256

# Okta sends the browser back to:
https://routes.example.com/callback?code=Q1w2...&state=Xy7...random

# Your server then POSTs code + client_secret + code_verifier
# to the token endpoint and receives id_token and access_token.

# --- Verifying the ID token (Python) ---
# Verifying an IdP's ID token: RS256 with the IdP's public keys (JWKS)
import jwt                                  # PyJWT, pip install "pyjwt[crypto]"
from jwt import PyJWKClient

ISSUER = "https://keelridge.okta.com/oauth2/default"
jwks = PyJWKClient(ISSUER + "/v1/keys")     # caches keys, refetches on a new kid

def verify_id_token(token: str, client_id: str) -> dict:
    key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)   # picks the key by the token's kid
    return jwt.decode(token, key.key,
                      algorithms=["RS256"],      # pinned: never read alg from the token
                      audience=client_id, issuer=ISSUER)

# Offline demo of the same checks with a key we make ourselves
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
priv = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
good = jwt.encode({"sub": "u-7", "aud": "app1", "iss": ISSUER}, priv,
                  algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": "k1"})
print(jwt.decode(good, priv.public_key(), algorithms=["RS256"],
                 audience="app1", issuer=ISSUER)["sub"])      # u-7

forged = jwt.encode({"sub": "admin", "aud": "app1", "iss": ISSUER},
                    None, algorithm="none")                    # alg=none attack
try:
    jwt.decode(forged, priv.public_key(), algorithms=["RS256"],
               audience="app1", issuer=ISSUER)
except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
    print("rejected:", type(e).__name__)   # rejected: InvalidAlgorithmError

replace_subtopics.title: Service accounts and secrets
replace_subtopics.body:
Not every caller is a person. A nightly pipeline, a worker or a CI job needs its own identity, called a service account. Give each one only the permissions it needs (least privilege), and never reuse a human's login for it.

The credentials themselves (API keys, database passwords, client secrets, signing keys) are secrets. They belong in a secrets manager such as AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault. The app reads them at runtime, access is logged, and they can be rotated without a code change.

In cloud environments, prefer identities with no long-lived secret at all: an IAM role attached to the compute, or workload identity federation, where the platform issues short-lived credentials automatically.

When one service calls another's API with OAuth, it uses the client-credentials grant. There is no user and no browser: the service sends its own client id and secret (or a signed assertion) to the token endpoint and gets a short-lived access token with narrow scopes. It caches the token until it nearly expires, then asks again.

When your product issues API keys to customers, treat them like passwords you cannot recover. Generate a long random key, show it to the user once, and store only a hash of it plus a short visible prefix (such as fk_3a9c1e07). The prefix lets you find the row, show "key ending ..." in the UI and spot leaked keys in logs or code scans. Rotation means issuing a second key, letting the customer switch over, then revoking the first, so allow two active keys per client.
replace_subtopics.example: Your ingestion job for a retailer needs to read one S3 bucket and write to one Postgres schema. You create a service role that can only s3:GetObject on that bucket, attach it to the ECS task, and store the Postgres password in Secrets Manager with 30-day rotation. A git scan later finds an old .env file with a key in history; you rotate that key immediately, because deleting the file does not remove it from history. The retailer's nightly sync now calls your API with its own client-credentials token (scope claims.read), and their partner uses an API key whose prefix appears in your audit log, never the full key.

import json, boto3

def get_db_password() -> str:
    # The task's IAM role grants secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
    # on this one secret only. No keys live in the code or image.
    sm = boto3.client("secretsmanager", region_name="eu-west-1")
    resp = sm.get_secret_value(SecretId="prod/ingest/postgres")
    return json.loads(resp["SecretString"])["password"]

# .gitignore should list: .env, *.pem, credentials.json
# Run a secret scanner (for example gitleaks) in CI before merge.

# --- Client credentials and hashed API keys ---
# 1) Machine-to-machine: the OAuth client-credentials grant
import httpx

def get_service_token() -> str:
    resp = httpx.post(
        "https://keelridge.okta.com/oauth2/default/v1/token",
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials", "scope": "claims.read"},
        auth=(CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET))      # both loaded from the vault
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()["access_token"]        # short-lived; cache until expiry

# 2) API keys you issue: show once, store only a hash, look up by prefix
import secrets, hashlib, hmac

def new_api_key():
    prefix = "fk_" + secrets.token_hex(4)               # visible, safe to log
    full = prefix + "." + secrets.token_urlsafe(32)     # shown to the user once
    row = {"prefix": prefix,
           "hash": hashlib.sha256(full.encode()).hexdigest()}
    return full, row

def check_key(presented, rows):
    row = rows.get(presented.split(".")[0])
    if not row:
        return False
    digest = hashlib.sha256(presented.encode()).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(digest, row["hash"])     # constant-time compare

key, row = new_api_key()
rows = {row["prefix"]: row}
print(len(key.split(".")[0]))             # 11
print(check_key(key, rows))               # True
print(check_key(key + "x", rows))         # False
# SHA-256 is fine here because the key is 32 random bytes nobody can guess;
# human passwords are guessable, so they need argon2 or bcrypt instead.

add_glossary: SCIM
A standard REST API an IdP uses to create, update and deactivate users in your app automatically.
JIT provisioning
Creating a user record the first time someone logs in through SSO.
CSRF
Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the browser send a request that carries your cookie.
SameSite
A cookie flag that stops the browser sending the cookie on requests started by other websites.
JWKS
JSON Web Key Set: the public keys an IdP publishes so apps can verify its signed tokens.
Passkey
A phishing-resistant login credential based on WebAuthn that only works on the real website domain.
argon2id
A slow, salted password hashing algorithm, the current first choice for storing passwords.
Client-credentials grant
The OAuth flow where a service gets a token with its own id and secret, with no user involved.
mTLS
Mutual TLS: both client and server present certificates, so each proves its identity.
DNS rebinding
An attack where a domain resolves to a safe IP at check time and an internal IP at connect time.

add_subtopics.title: Detecting and redacting PII in text and logs
add_subtopics.body:
Regex finds things with a fixed shape: emails, phone numbers, card and social security numbers. It cannot find names, addresses or a diagnosis written in a sentence. For those you need named entity recognition (NER), a model that tags spans of text as PERSON, LOCATION and so on. The usual open-source tool is Microsoft Presidio, which combines regex, checksums and an NER model and returns each finding with a type and a confidence score. The cloud equivalents are Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection (DLP), Amazon Comprehend PII detection and Azure AI Language PII detection.

No detector is perfect, so measure it. Hand-label 100 to 200 real examples from the customer's data (support tickets, chat logs), run the detector, and compute recall: of all the real PII, what share did it find? Look at every miss. Typical misses are lowercase names, addresses and ids in the customer's own format, and you fix them with extra rules or a stricter policy. Report the number to the customer: 'recall 97 percent on 150 labelled tickets' is an answer a privacy officer can work with.

Then choose what to do with each finding. Mask it ([PERSON]) when nobody needs it again. Use reversible pseudonymisation when a later step must restore it: replace the value with a stable token and keep the token-to-value map in a locked vault, so the LLM sees P_3f9a... and your app swaps the real name back in the final answer. Apply the same redaction before text reaches logs and traces.
add_subtopics.example: Fernhollow Surveys wants to send 40,000 support chats to an LLM for tagging. You run Presidio on 150 labelled chats: recall is 91 percent, with most misses being lowercase names typed by customers. After adding a lowercase-name rule and a postcode pattern, recall reaches 98 percent. The chats go to the model with stable tokens in place of names, and the dashboard shows real names only to staff allowed to see them.

# pip install presidio-analyzer presidio-anonymizer
# python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm   (use _lg in production)
import hmac, hashlib
from presidio_analyzer import AnalyzerEngine
from presidio_analyzer.nlp_engine import NlpEngineProvider

nlp = NlpEngineProvider(nlp_configuration={
    "nlp_engine_name": "spacy",
    "models": [{"lang_code": "en", "model_name": "en_core_web_sm"}]}).create_engine()
analyzer = AnalyzerEngine(nlp_engine=nlp)
WANTED = ["PERSON", "EMAIL_ADDRESS", "PHONE_NUMBER", "US_SSN"]

def find_pii(text):
    hits = analyzer.analyze(text=text, language="en", entities=WANTED)
    return [(h.entity_type, text[h.start:h.end]) for h in hits if h.score >= 0.4]

text = "Please call Maria Lopez on 212-555-0199 or email maria.lopez@fernhollow.com"
for kind, value in sorted(find_pii(text)):
    print(kind, "->", value)   # exact hits depend on the spaCy model
# EMAIL_ADDRESS -> maria.lopez@fernhollow.com
# PERSON -> Maria Lopez
# PHONE_NUMBER -> 212-555-0199

# Measure recall on a small hand-labelled sample: of the real PII, how much did we find?
labelled = [
    ("Ticket from John Carter, phone 415-555-0133", {"John Carter", "415-555-0133"}),
    ("Refund sent to priya.n@fernhollow.com today", {"priya.n@fernhollow.com"}),
    ("Spoke to Dr. Amara Okafor about the claim", {"Amara Okafor"}),
    ("chat log: hi its ben ruiz, my card was charged twice", {"ben ruiz"}),
    ("Deliver to 14 Elm Road, Leeds LS6 2AB", {"14 Elm Road, Leeds LS6 2AB"}),
]
found = missed = 0
for text, truth in labelled:
    got = {v for _, v in find_pii(text)}
    for item in truth:
        if any(item in g for g in got):          # the whole value must be covered
            found += 1
        else:
            missed += 1
            print("MISSED:", item)
print(f"recall = {found}/{found + missed}")
# MISSED: ben ruiz
# MISSED: 14 Elm Road, Leeds LS6 2AB
# recall = 4/6   (lowercase names and addresses slip through: add rules or review)

# Reversible pseudonymisation: same person -> same token, and only the vault maps back
KEY = b"load-from-secrets-manager"
vault = {}                                     # token -> original, kept in a locked store
def pseudonymise(value):
    token = "P_" + hmac.new(KEY, value.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:10]
    vault[token] = value
    return token

print(t1 == t2, t1.startswith("P_"))           # True True
print(vault[t1])                               # Maria Lopez

replace_subtopics.title: PII, PHI and data classification
replace_subtopics.body:
Start by knowing what kind of data you hold. Direct identifiers point to one person on their own: name, email, social security number, passport number. Indirect identifiers can identify someone in combination: date of birth plus zip code plus gender. Both count as PII in most frameworks.

PHI is health information (diagnoses, lab results, appointment dates, insurance ids) held by a healthcare provider, health plan or their business partners and linked to a person. HIPAA lists 18 identifiers that must be removed for data to count as de-identified under its Safe Harbor method.

A data classification scheme sorts data into levels, and each level gets rules. Most companies use four or so levels. Ask the customer for their scheme and use their names for the levels.

Two words are mixed up constantly: pseudonymisation and anonymisation. Pseudonymised data has the names swapped for tokens, hashes or ids, but someone holding the key, a lookup table or a list of candidates can link it back to the person. Under GDPR pseudonymised data is still personal data, and all the rules still apply. It lowers the risk, which regulators like, but it does not take the data out of scope. Hashing an email is only pseudonymisation, because anyone can hash a list of known emails and match them.

Anonymised data cannot be linked back to a person by anyone using reasonable means, even when combined with other data. Only then is it outside GDPR. True anonymisation usually means removing ids and indirect identifiers and sharing only aggregates over groups big enough to hide one person. When a customer says 'we will send you anonymised data', ask how it was done; usually it is pseudonymised.

The regex redactor below is only a first pass. The next subtopic shows a real PII detector and how to measure what it misses.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer sends you three files. products.csv lists policy types and prices: Internal. customers.csv has names, emails and addresses: Confidential PII. claims_medical.csv has diagnosis codes per claimant: Restricted PHI. You store the first in the shared bucket, the second in an encrypted bucket with a small access group, and the third only in the customer's own environment, because your contract does not cover PHI yet. Their data team then offers to 'anonymise' the customer file by hashing emails. You explain that this is pseudonymisation, so the file stays Confidential PII under your DPA, and you ask for regional totals instead where the pilot does not need row-level data.

import re

PATTERNS = {
    "email": re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+"),
    "us_ssn": re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b"),
    "phone": re.compile(r"\+?\d[\d\s().-]{8,}\d"),
}

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    # A simple first pass. Real projects add a proper PII detector
    # and human review, since regex misses names and addresses.
    for label, pat in PATTERNS.items():
        text = pat.sub(f"[{label.upper()}]", text)
    return text

print(redact("Call Ann at +1 415 555 0100 or ann@example.com, SSN 123-45-6789"))

# --- Pseudonymised is not anonymous ---
# Hashing an email is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation:
# anyone with a list of emails can hash them and match the rows again.

h = lambda email: hashlib.sha256(email.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

staff_list = ["bob@fernhollow.com", "ann@fernhollow.com"]
lookup = {h(e): e for e in staff_list}

for region, amount in spend:
    groups.setdefault(region, []).append(amount)

replace_subtopics.title: GDPR, HIPAA and SOC 2
replace_subtopics.body:
GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is an EU law covering the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the company is based. Key ideas: you need a lawful basis to process data, collect only what you need (data minimization), honor rights such as access and erasure, and report certain breaches to the regulator within 72 hours. A controller decides why data is processed; a processor handles it on the controller's behalf. As a vendor you are usually a processor.

HIPAA is a US law for health data. Covered entities (providers, health plans) and their business associates (vendors handling PHI for them) must protect PHI with administrative, physical and technical safeguards. A vendor must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) before receiving PHI.

SOC 2 is an audit report from an independent CPA firm, based on the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria: security, plus optionally availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Type I checks that controls are designed well at one point in time. Type II checks they operated over a period, often six to twelve months.

These rules also shape what you do when something goes wrong on site. If you suspect a data incident (a public bucket, a leaked key, personal data sent to the wrong system), the first hour matters most. Stop the spread: revoke the key, close the bucket, pause the job. Preserve evidence: do not delete logs or files, and write down times and what you saw. Escalate at once to the named security contact on both sides, as written in the contract or runbook. Do not investigate alone for days, and do not tell the customer's staff informally what you think happened; notification goes through the agreed channel. The reason for speed is the clock: under GDPR a controller must notify the regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, and as a processor you must tell the controller without undue delay. HIPAA and many contracts set their own deadlines too.
replace_subtopics.example: A US health startup with EU clinics evaluates your product. Their compliance lead asks for: a signed BAA (HIPAA, because you will process PHI), a DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses (GDPR, for the EU clinics' patient data), and your latest SOC 2 Type II report under NDA (proof your controls work). Three different documents for three different questions. On a Friday afternoon you notice a debug export of patient notes sitting in a shared drive. You remove the sharing link, note the time and the file path, keep the file, and call the security contact named in the runbook within 15 minutes. You do not email the clinic's staff yourself.

replace_subtopics.title: Least privilege and audit logs
replace_subtopics.body:
Least privilege means every person and service gets the minimum access needed for their task, for the shortest time needed. It limits the damage of a mistake or a stolen credential.

In practice: separate roles for reading and writing, no shared admin accounts, production access granted temporarily with an approval, and service accounts scoped to exactly the tables or buckets they use. Review access on a schedule and remove what is no longer needed.

Audit logs record who did what, to which resource, when, and from where. They must be append-only or tamper-evident, kept for the period the customer requires, and stored separately from the data they describe. Auditors and incident responders rely on them.

Keeping data forever is also a risk, so every data class needs a written retention period: for example chat transcripts 90 days, application logs 30 days, audit logs 1 year, signed contracts 7 years. The customer's policy and the law set the numbers; your job is to write them down per data store and enforce them with an automatic deletion job, not a reminder in someone's calendar. Deletion must reach copies too: caches, exports and search indexes.

The one exception is a legal hold. When there is a lawsuit, investigation or dispute, legal can order that certain data is kept even past its retention period. The deletion job must check the hold list and skip those records, and only legal removes a hold.
replace_subtopics.example: At a retailer, an FDE needs to debug an order pipeline. Instead of a permanent admin login, she requests read-only access to the orders schema for four hours through the access tool. Her manager approves. Every query she runs lands in the audit log. When the window ends, the grant expires by itself. In the quarterly review, the auditor samples this grant and finds the approval and the log. The retailer's policy says order-support chats are kept 90 days. Your nightly job deletes older transcripts, skips the two customers under legal hold, and writes how many rows it removed to the audit log.

replace_subtopics.title: Answering a security questionnaire
replace_subtopics.body:
Before signing, most enterprises send a security questionnaire. It may be their own spreadsheet or a standard one such as the SIG from Shared Assessments or the CAIQ from the Cloud Security Alliance. It can have a hundred questions or more.

The questions fall into predictable groups: company and certifications, access control and SSO, encryption, network security, vulnerability management and penetration tests, incident response, business continuity and backups, data retention and deletion, subprocessors, employee security training, and more and more often AI use.

Most companies keep a library of approved answers owned by the security team. As an FDE you help with the technical questions about your specific deployment. Be precise, point to evidence, and when the answer is 'no' or 'partially', say so and describe the compensating control or plan.

Many vendors now run a trust center (or trust portal): a web page where prospects can read security documents and, after accepting an NDA, download the SOC 2 report, pen test summary and policies. Point the customer there first; it answers half the questionnaire.

SOC 2 reports cover a fixed period, so there is often a gap between the end of the last period and today. A bridge letter (also called a gap letter) is a short signed statement from the vendor that no material changes to controls have happened since the report period ended. Customers ask for it when the report is more than a few months old.

One process rule for FDEs: never answer from memory, and never send answers straight to the customer. Draft technical answers for your deployment, then route every answer through the security team, who check it against the approved answer library and the signed contracts.
replace_subtopics.example: Question 47 asks: 'Is customer data used to train AI models?' A weak answer is 'No.' A strong answer: 'Customer data is not used to train models. Our LLM provider processes requests under an enterprise agreement that excludes training on inputs and retains data for a limited period for abuse monitoring, as stated in section 4 of our AI data use policy (attached).' The details must match the actual contract. The bank's report period ended in December and it is now May, so their vendor manager asks for a bridge letter. You request it from your security team together with your drafted answers, rather than writing it yourself.

replace_subtopics.title: Healthcare: HIPAA, BAAs, PHI and FHIR
replace_subtopics.body:
HIPAA is the US law for health information. It applies to covered entities (health providers, health plans and clearinghouses) and to their business associates, the vendors who handle protected health information (PHI) for them. PHI is health information that can be linked to a person, such as a diagnosis next to a name, a date of birth or a medical record number. Before any vendor receives PHI, it must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). That includes every subprocessor in the chain, such as your cloud host and your LLM provider.

Two rules shape daily work. The minimum necessary standard says you use only the PHI needed for the task. De-identified data is no longer PHI; HIPAA allows two methods: Safe Harbor, which removes 18 listed identifiers, or Expert Determination by a qualified statistician.

Hospital data usually arrives through HL7 standards. HL7 v2 is an older pipe-delimited message format (for example an ADT message when a patient is admitted). FHIR is the modern REST API, with JSON resources such as Patient, Observation and Encounter. Many electronic health record systems now expose FHIR APIs, usually secured with OAuth 2.0 scopes.

There is a middle option between full PHI and de-identified data: the Limited Data Set. It removes direct identifiers such as names, street addresses, phone numbers, emails and record numbers, but it may keep dates (admission, discharge, birth), town, state and ZIP code. It is still PHI, so it cannot be shared freely, but it can be shared for research, public health or health care operations under a Data Use Agreement (DUA). The DUA says what the data may be used for, bans re-identifying people and bans passing it on. It is a good fit when a pilot needs dates, for example to measure time from admission to discharge, but does not need to know who the patient is.

When an app talks to an electronic health record, the standard way to get a FHIR token is SMART on FHIR. It is a profile of OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. The app asks for scopes that name the resource type and the action, such as patient/DocumentReference.read (only this patient's documents) or user/Observation.read (what the signed-in clinician may see). A backend service without a user uses SMART Backend Services, signing in with a private key instead of a password. Ask for the narrowest scopes that do the job; the hospital's EHR team will check them.
replace_subtopics.example: Lindqvale Health wants an assistant that summarises discharge notes. The FDE asks for a FHIR scope limited to DocumentReference and Encounter, not the full Patient record, and checks that the hosting cloud and the model provider both have signed BAAs. The patient's name and address are not needed for a summary, so the pipeline drops them before the prompt is built. For a length-of-stay study, the FDE asks Lindqvale for a Limited Data Set under a Data Use Agreement instead of full records: dates and ZIP codes stay, names and record numbers go. For the live summariser, the app registers as a SMART on FHIR app and asks only for the patient/DocumentReference.read scope.

replace_subtopics.title: Finance: SOC 2, PCI DSS, SOX and model risk
replace_subtopics.body:
Banks, insurers and fintechs will ask for your SOC 2 Type II report first. It shows an auditor tested your controls over a period, often six to twelve months. Expect to hand over evidence: access reviews, change tickets, incident records.

PCI DSS is the payment card industry's security standard. It applies to any system that stores, processes or transmits card data, called the cardholder data environment (CDE). Every system connected to the CDE is 'in scope' and must meet the controls. The best move is scope reduction: replace the card number (PAN) with a token from a payment provider, so your AI system never sees real card numbers and stays out of scope. Card security codes must never be stored after authorisation. The standard is versioned (4.0 and later); check the current version.

SOX is a US law for public companies. For engineers it means IT general controls around financial systems: approved and tested changes, segregation of duties (the person who writes code does not deploy it alone) and access reviews.

Model risk management, described in US bank supervisors' guidance SR 11-7, expects every model that drives decisions to be documented, independently validated and monitored. Banks increasingly treat LLM features as models under this process.

EU banks, insurers and payment firms now also cite DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, which has applied since 17 January 2025. It is about staying up and recovering when technology fails, and it reaches their technology vendors, which includes an AI vendor. Expect three things. First, the customer must keep a register of all ICT third-party providers, so they will ask what you run, where and with which subprocessors. Second, contracts for important services need exit plans: how the customer could move to another provider or bring the work in-house, and how they get their data back. Third, major ICT incidents must be reported to the regulator on tight deadlines, so your contract will require you to tell the customer about incidents quickly, with details. Some large providers can even be named 'critical' and overseen directly by EU supervisors.
replace_subtopics.example: Pemberly Mutual wants an agent that answers billing questions. The FDE designs it to see only a token such as tok_8f3k and the last four digits, never the full card number. The payment provider stays the only system in PCI scope, and the agent needs no PCI assessment. For SOX, every prompt change goes through a pull request approved by a second engineer. A Dublin payments firm adds a DORA annex to the contract. The FDE supplies the list of subprocessors and regions for the register, a one-page exit plan (export of prompts, outputs and embeddings in open formats within 30 days) and the incident contact who will call them within hours.

replace_subtopics.title: Data residency and cross-border transfer
replace_subtopics.body:
Data residency means where data is stored and processed. The EU's GDPR does not ban moving personal data out of the EU, but a transfer needs a legal basis: an adequacy decision for the destination country, Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) with a transfer assessment, or Binding Corporate Rules. For the US, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework covers companies that certify under it. These mechanisms have been challenged in court before, so check the current position.

A DPIA (data protection impact assessment) is required before high-risk processing, which many AI projects on personal data are. In California, the CCPA as amended by the CPRA gives consumers rights to know, delete, correct, and opt out of the sale or sharing of their data. Vendors act as 'service providers' under a contract.

For an FDE the practical questions are: which region hosts every copy of the data, including logs, backups, vector indexes, evaluation sets and the model provider's endpoint? And when a person asks to be deleted, can you remove their chunks from the vector store and their prompts from the logs? If the answer is 'we are not sure', fix it before launch.

Regulated customers usually ask about the EU AI Act in the same review. The Act sorts AI systems by risk. Some uses are listed as high-risk: credit scoring of people, pricing of life and health insurance, screening job applicants and some medical uses. High-risk systems need risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and documentation, and the rules phase in over several years, so check the current dates. If the customer's use case is on that list, expect their legal team to want to know who is the 'provider' and who is the 'deployer'. The responsibleai lesson covers the Act in detail; here, just spot the trigger and bring in their legal team early.
replace_subtopics.example: Veltrana Insurance, based in Germany, wants all personal data processed in the EU. The FDE picks an EU region for the database and vector store and an EU-hosted model endpoint, turns off prompt logging in a US tool, and stores each chunk with a customer_id so a deletion request can remove every chunk for that person. When Veltrana mentions using the same assistant to help price health cover, the FDE flags that insurance pricing is a high-risk use under the EU AI Act and asks their legal team to join the next design review.

replace_subtopics.title: How an FDE works inside these rules
replace_subtopics.body:
Treat compliance as a design input from day one. In week one, find out which frameworks apply, who the customer's compliance and security contacts are, and which data classes your system will touch. Then shape the design so the fewest systems are in scope: tokenise, de-identify, keep data in the right region and log access.

Ask for sample data early, and expect to receive synthetic or de-identified data first. Plan for reviews: a security review, a privacy review, sometimes a model risk review. They take weeks, so start them in parallel with the build.

Keep an evidence folder as you go: architecture diagram, data-flow diagram, list of subprocessors, access list, test results. When the auditor or the customer's risk team asks, you answer in hours. Never say 'we are compliant' without naming the framework and scope. Say what is true, for example 'our SOC 2 Type II report covers this service; the model provider has signed a BAA with us'. The table below is a quick map from framework to what changes in your deployment.

Life sciences and pharma are a big market for FDEs, and they bring their own rules, called GxP (good practice rules for manufacturing, labs and clinical trials). In the US, 21 CFR Part 11 covers electronic records and electronic signatures. In practice it means three things. The system must be validated: written requirements, test scripts and signed evidence that it does what it should, redone when it changes. Every create, change or delete of a record must go into a secure, time-stamped audit trail that users cannot edit. And an electronic signature must be tied to one person and record what they signed and why. A model that changes behind an API makes validation harder, so pin versions and keep test evidence.
replace_subtopics.example: At a regional bank, the FDE starts the model risk review in week two with a one-page model card, rather than waiting until the pilot ends. The review finishes the same week the pilot does, and go-live is not delayed. A vaccine maker wants help drafting batch deviation reports. The FDE pins the model version, writes a validation test pack with 40 cases, and makes sure every draft the reviewer approves is signed and logged in the customer's validated quality system, not in the assistant.

replace_subtopics.title: Structured logging
replace_subtopics.body:
A log line written as free text, like 'Failed to process order', is hard to search and impossible to count. Structured logging writes each event as a set of named fields, usually JSON. Now you can filter for event=order_failed and customer=fernhollow.

Every log line should carry a request id (or trace id) that is created at the edge and passed through every service. That single field lets you pull together everything that happened for one request.

Use log levels with meaning: DEBUG for detail you only want while investigating, INFO for normal business events, WARNING for something odd but handled, ERROR for a failed operation. Never log passwords, tokens or raw PII.

Do not pass the request id by hand to every function. In Python, store it in a contextvars.ContextVar. A small middleware sets it once when the request arrives (reusing an incoming X-Request-ID header if there is one), and the log formatter reads it for every line. Each request, even with async code, sees only its own value. Also write the OpenTelemetry trace_id into each log line; then a log line links straight to its trace and back.

Write timestamps in UTC in ISO-8601 format, such as 2026-09-29T08:15:02.113+00:00. Local time with no zone breaks when servers sit in different regions or clocks change for summer time.

Where do logs go? In containers, the app writes one JSON line per event to stdout, and the platform collects it (a Kubernetes node agent, or the cloud's log driver). From there it is shipped to a log store: Loki or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (the ELK stack) if you run your own, or CloudWatch Logs, Google Cloud Logging, Azure Monitor or Datadog as services. Log stores charge by volume ingested and by retention days, so decide both: for example 14 days searchable, 1 year in cheap archive storage for audits. DEBUG logging left on in production is a common surprise on the bill.
replace_subtopics.example: A claims API at an insurer processes 50,000 requests a day. A customer calls about claim 44718. Support searches the logs for claim_id=44718, finds request_id=r-8f3a, and then filters on that id to see all five lines from the API, the fraud check service and the database layer, including the one with level=error and reason=timeout. At the insurer, the log store bill doubles in a month. The team finds DEBUG lines from a retry loop, turns production back to INFO, and sets 14 days of hot retention with 365 days in archive, which the customer's audit team signed off.

import logging, json, uuid, contextvars
from datetime import datetime, timezone

# One value per request (or per asyncio task); middleware sets it once
request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default="-")

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        base = {"ts": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds"),
                "level": record.levelname, "msg": record.getMessage(),
                "request_id": request_id.get()}          # added to every line
        base.update(getattr(record, "fields", {}))   # extra named fields
        return json.dumps(base)

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
log = logging.getLogger("claims"); log.addHandler(handler); log.setLevel("INFO")

def handle_request(claim_id):          # in FastAPI this is done by middleware
    request_id.set(str(uuid.uuid4())[:8])
    log.info("claim_received", extra={"fields": {"claim_id": claim_id}})
    log.error("fraud_check_timeout", extra={"fields": {"after_ms": 5000}})

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next):

    finally:

    return format(ctx.trace_id, "032x") if ctx.is_valid else "-"

replace_subtopics.title: Metrics with RED and USE
replace_subtopics.body:
A metric is a number with a name, labels and a time. Three common types: a counter only goes up (total requests), a gauge goes up and down (queue length), and a histogram groups measurements into buckets so you can compute percentiles (request duration).

Two checklists tell you what to measure. RED is for services that handle requests: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second or as a share), Duration (how long they take). USE is for resources like CPU, memory, disks and connection pools: Utilization (how busy), Saturation (how much work is waiting), Errors.

Look at latency as percentiles. The p95 is the time under which 95% of requests finish. Averages hide the slow tail that angry users experience.

Be careful with labels. Every different combination of label values creates a new time series that Prometheus keeps in memory. A label like route has maybe 20 values, which is fine. A label like user_id, request_id, email or the full URL with ids in it can have millions of values. That is called high cardinality, and it slows queries, fills memory and raises the bill on hosted metrics services. Keep metric labels to small, fixed sets (route template, status class, region, model name). Put per-user or per-request detail in logs or trace attributes, where it belongs.
replace_subtopics.example: An e-commerce checkout service shows an average latency of 180 ms, which looks fine. The p99 is 4.2 seconds. The histogram shows a cluster of slow requests only for customers with more than 50 items in the cart, which leads straight to an unindexed query. An FDE adds a customer_id label to the LLM token counter for 40,000 end users; Prometheus memory triples in a day. They change the label to plan (free, pro, enterprise) and keep customer_id in the trace attributes instead.

from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server

REQS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Requests", ["route", "status"])
LAT = Histogram("http_request_seconds", "Request duration", ["route"])

def handle_checkout(cart):

        status = process(cart)
    REQS.labels(route="/checkout", status=str(status)).inc()  # Rate, Errors

replace_subtopics.title: Distributed tracing
replace_subtopics.body:
A modern request often touches many services: an API gateway, your app, a search index, a database, an LLM. A trace records the whole journey. It is made of spans; each span is one unit of work with a start time, a duration, a name and attributes. Spans nest: the 'handle request' span contains a 'query database' span and a 'call LLM' span.

The trace id is passed from service to service in a header (the W3C traceparent header is the standard), so every service adds its spans to the same trace.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the open standard and set of SDKs for producing logs, metrics and traces in a vendor-neutral way. You instrument once and can send the data to Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb or another backend.

You rarely write every span by hand. Auto-instrumentation libraries add spans for common frameworks: FastAPIInstrumentor for incoming requests, and the requests, httpx and database driver instrumentors for outgoing calls. You can even run an unchanged app with the opentelemetry-instrument command, which switches them all on. You then add manual spans only for your own important steps, like retrieve or rerank.

Apps usually send spans to the OpenTelemetry Collector, not straight to a vendor. The Collector is a separate service that receives data (usually over OTLP), processes it (batching, removing sensitive attributes, sampling) and exports it to one or more backends. Changing vendor then means changing Collector config, not app code.

Tracing every request can be expensive at high volume, so you sample. Head-based sampling decides at the start of a trace, for example keep 10% of traces at random. It is cheap but may drop the one slow or failed request you need. Tail-based sampling waits until the trace is finished and then decides, so you can keep every trace with an error or over 2 seconds plus a small share of normal ones. The Collector does tail sampling, which needs all spans of a trace to reach the same Collector instance.
replace_subtopics.example: A support-bot request takes 9 seconds. The trace shows: retrieve documents 300 ms, rerank 200 ms, LLM call 1.8 s, then a second LLM call 6.5 s. The second call was a retry after a timeout on the first attempt. The fix is a shorter first timeout and streaming, which you would never have guessed from the total alone. A support bot handles 3 million requests a day and the tracing bill is high. The team keeps 5% of normal traces but, using tail sampling in the Collector, keeps 100% of traces with an error or longer than 5 seconds. Cost falls by about 90% and no failed request is lost.

from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor, ConsoleSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("support-bot")

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("answer") as span:      # parent span
        span.set_attribute("question.length", len(question))
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve"):        # child span
            docs = search(question)
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("llm.generate"):    # child span
            return generate(question, docs)

replace_subtopics.title: Alerts, on-call and runbooks
replace_subtopics.body:
An alert is a rule that notifies a person when something needs action. A good alert is about a symptom users feel, is actionable, and is rare. Pages (which wake someone up) are for urgent user impact. Everything else goes to a ticket or a chat channel.

On-call means a named person is responsible for responding during a period. When paged, they acknowledge, assess impact, mitigate first (roll back, fail over, turn off a feature flag) and investigate the root cause after users are safe.

A runbook is a short document linked from the alert. It says what the alert means, how to check it, the common causes and the safe first actions. After an incident, a blameless postmortem records the timeline, the cause and the follow-up fixes without blaming people.

A single threshold alert on the error rate either fires too late or too often. The SRE approach is multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting on the SLO. The burn rate says how fast the error budget is being spent: 1x means exactly on plan for the window. A common page rule for a 30-day SLO is: burn rate above 14.4x over the last hour AND over the last 5 minutes. 14.4x for one hour spends 2% of the monthly budget, which is serious. The short window makes the alert stop soon after the problem is fixed. A slower rule (for example 6x over 6 hours and 30 minutes) opens a ticket instead of paging.

Two more tools complete the picture. Error tracking tools such as Sentry catch exceptions with the stack trace, the release and the number of users hit, and group repeats of the same bug. Synthetic or uptime checks call your public endpoint from outside your network every minute, so you notice when DNS, TLS certificates or the load balancer fail, which your own metrics may never see.
replace_subtopics.example: At 02:10 an alert fires: checkout error rate above 2% for 10 minutes. The on-call engineer opens the linked runbook, checks the dashboard, and sees errors started with the 01:55 deploy. The runbook's step 2 says roll back the last deploy. Errors drop at 02:18. The next day the postmortem finds a missing database migration and adds a deploy check. The checkout team replaces its 2% error alert with burn-rate rules for a 99.9% SLO. A short 3-minute blip no longer pages anyone, but a steady 2% error rate (20x burn) pages after about 45 minutes, and a full outage pages in about a minute. An outside uptime check also catches an expired TLS certificate that internal metrics missed.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Prometheus alerting rule
groups:
- name: checkout
  rules:
  - alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
    expr: |
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
        / sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[5m])) > 0.02
    for: 10m                          # must persist, avoids flapping
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout 5xx rate above 2% for 10 minutes"
      runbook_url: "https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/checkout-errors"

# Multi-window burn-rate page for a 99.9% SLO (budget 0.001)
  - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
    expr: |
      (sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout",status=~"5.."}[1h]))
        / sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[1h]))) > (14.4 * 0.001)
      and
      (sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
        / sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[5m]))) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    labels:
      severity: page

Alert links to a runbook
Runbook: what it means, how to confirm, first safe actions
Dashboard link shows the relevant RED metrics
Escalation path and owner are written down
Postmortem template ready: timeline, impact, cause, actions
Page on fast SLO burn (1h and 5m windows), ticket on slow burn
Exceptions go to an error tracker with the release tagged
An outside uptime check hits the public URL every minute

replace_subtopics.title: Tracing LLM calls
replace_subtopics.body:
LLM features need the same signals plus some of their own. For each model call, record the model name, the prompt template version, input and output token counts, latency (including time to first token when streaming), cost, the stop reason, and any tool calls with their results.

Agents make many calls per user request, so traces matter even more. A trace shows the chain: plan, tool call, retrieval, second model call, final answer. Without it, a bad answer is a mystery.

OpenTelemetry has semantic conventions for generative AI with attribute names such as gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, and several LLM observability tools (for example Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix) build on traces. Store full prompts and outputs only if your data policy allows it, since they may contain customer PII.

Traces become far more useful when quality signals are attached to them. Return the trace id to the UI with each answer. When the user clicks thumbs up or down, send that score to your tracing tool keyed by the trace id. Add automatic signals too: an LLM judge or eval score, whether a guardrail fired (PII found, off-topic, blocked tool), and whether the user retried. Now you can filter for 'thumbs down on prompt v15' and open each bad trace. The llmobs lesson goes deeper into LLM observability and production feedback.

Prompts and outputs often hold customer data, so decide a policy: redact PII before storing, store full bodies only for a sample, or keep only token counts and hashes for regulated customers.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims assistant costs twice the forecast. The traces show that 30% of requests call the retrieval tool three times because the model keeps rephrasing the query. Grouping by prompt version shows it started with version 14. Reverting the prompt halves tokens per request, and a dashboard of cost per request by prompt version now catches this kind of change. The insurer's assistant sends thumbs-down clicks with the trace id. A weekly review of the 50 worst traces shows most come from one policy document with a broken table, which was invisible in latency or cost dashboards.

import time
from anthropic import Anthropic
from opentelemetry import trace

MODEL = "MODEL"   # put the current model id here
client, tracer = Anthropic(), trace.get_tracer("claims-assistant")

def ask(question: str, prompt_version="v15") -> tuple[str, str]:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("llm.chat") as span:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        msg = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=800,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", MODEL)
        span.set_attribute("prompt.version", prompt_version)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", msg.usage.input_tokens)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", msg.usage.output_tokens)
        span.set_attribute("llm.stop_reason", msg.stop_reason)
        span.set_attribute("llm.latency_ms", int((time.monotonic() - t0) * 1000))
        text = "".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")
        # Quality signals travel with the trace too
        span.set_attribute("guardrail.pii_found", "@" in text)   # toy check
        trace_id = format(span.get_span_context().trace_id, "032x")
        return text, trace_id          # the UI keeps trace_id for feedback

def record_feedback(trace_id: str, thumbs_up: bool, judge_score: float | None = None):
    # Send to your LLM observability tool (for example Langfuse's score API)
    # keyed by trace_id, so a thumbs down opens the exact trace.
    print({"trace_id": trace_id, "user_feedback": 1 if thumbs_up else 0,
           "judge_score": judge_score})

add_subtopics.title: Finding the bottleneck before you cache
add_subtopics.body:
'Measure first' is the golden rule, and here is how. A cache hides a slow step; it does not fix it, and it adds staleness and another system to run. So find out where the time really goes.

Start with a trace or timing log of one slow request to see which step is slow: your Python code, the database, or an outside API. If it is Python, profile it. cProfile is built in and counts every function call and its time. py-spy attaches to a running process without code changes (py-spy top --pid 1234, or py-spy record to make a flame graph), which is handy in production.

If it is the database, ask the database. In PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows the plan with real times and row counts. A 'Seq Scan' over a big table where you expected an index is the classic find, and an index often beats any cache.

Watch for the N+1 query problem: code loads a list with one query, then runs one more query per item in a loop. It is fast with 10 rows in testing and slow with 2,000 in production. ORMs cause it easily. The fix is one query with a JOIN, or the ORM's eager loading (select_related or selectinload).

Finally check connection pools. If the app has 20 workers but the database pool allows 5 connections, requests wait in line for a connection, and the database looks idle while users wait. Size the pool to what the database can serve, and watch pool wait time as a USE saturation metric.
add_subtopics.example: A wholesaler's monthly report takes 40 seconds and the team wants to cache it. The FDE profiles it first: 2,001 database queries, one per customer. Rewriting it as one JOIN query brings it to 0.3 seconds, so no cache is needed at all.
add_subtopics.code:
# Profile first: an N+1 query loop hidden in a report function
import cProfile, pstats, sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, total REAL);
""")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO customers VALUES (?, ?)", [(i, f"c{i}") for i in range(2000)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(i, i % 2000, 10.0) for i in range(20000)])

def report_slow():                      # 1 query + 1 query per customer = N+1
    out = {}
    for (cid, name) in db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM customers").fetchall():
        out[name] = db.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?",
                               (cid,)).fetchone()[0]
    return out

def report_fast():                      # one query with a JOIN and GROUP BY
    rows = db.execute("""SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total) FROM customers c
                         JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id""")
    return dict(rows.fetchall())

assert report_slow() == report_fast()
prof = cProfile.Profile(); prof.enable(); report_slow(); prof.disable()
stats = pstats.Stats(prof).sort_stats("cumulative")
calls = [v[1] for k, v in stats.stats.items() if k[2] == "<method 'execute' of 'sqlite3.Connection' objects>"][0]
print("execute() calls in report_slow:", calls)
# execute() calls in report_slow: 2001   -> one query per customer: N+1
# stats.print_stats(5) shows the top 5 functions by time

# PostgreSQL: ask the planner what really happens
# EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
#   Seq Scan on orders (actual time=0.02..85.1 rows=10 loops=1)  <- no index used
# CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);   -> Index Scan, about 0.05 ms
# Running process:  py-spy top --pid 1234

Profile Python with cProfile or py-spy
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow queries and check for missing indexes
Count queries per request to catch N+1 loops
Check pool size and pool wait time
Only then decide whether a cache is the right fix

replace_subtopics.title: Where caches live
replace_subtopics.body:
The browser cache keeps files and responses on the user's device, controlled by the Cache-Control header your server sends. Static files like images and scripts can be cached for a long time if their file name changes when their content changes.

A CDN (content delivery network) such as CloudFront, Cloudflare or Fastly keeps copies on servers near users. It serves static files and sometimes whole API responses that are the same for everyone.

Inside your system, an application cache can be an in-process dictionary (fast, but each server has its own copy and it vanishes on restart) or a shared store like Redis or Memcached. Databases cache too: their buffer pool keeps hot pages in memory, and you can build materialized views or summary tables to precompute heavy results.

In Python, the simplest in-process cache is functools.lru_cache. It keeps the results of recent calls and throws out the least recently used ones when full. It has no expiry time, so it is good for values that never change while the process runs, like a table of tax rates. For values that do change, use cachetools.TTLCache, which also expires entries after a set number of seconds.

Remember that a web server usually runs several worker processes, maybe on several machines. Each has its own in-process cache, filled at different times. After a price change, one worker may show the new price and another the old one until its entry expires. If users must see the same value everywhere, use a shared cache such as Redis.
replace_subtopics.example: A news site for a publisher: article images and JavaScript are cached for a year in browsers and at the CDN (file names include a content hash). The article HTML is cached at the CDN for 60 seconds. Comment counts come from Redis with a 30-second TTL. The logged-in user's reading history is never cached at shared layers. The publisher's app caches its list of section names with lru_cache, because it changes only on deploy, and caches exchange rates with a 60-second TTLCache. Stock levels, which must match across servers, go through Redis.

# Public page: CDN may keep 60 s, browser must revalidate

# Personal data: never store in shared caches

# Revalidation: the browser sends If-None-Match with this value,
# the server replies 304 Not Modified if nothing changed
ETag: "a7f3c9"

# --- In-process caches in Python ---
# In-process caches in Python
import time
from functools import lru_cache
from cachetools import TTLCache, cached

@lru_cache(maxsize=1024)            # keeps up to 1,024 results, never expires
def tax_rate(country: str) -> float:
    print("  loading", country)
    return {"DE": 0.19, "FR": 0.20}[country]

tax_rate("DE"); tax_rate("DE")      # loads once
print(tax_rate.cache_info())        # CacheInfo(hits=1, misses=1, maxsize=1024, currsize=1)

@cached(TTLCache(maxsize=1024, ttl=2))   # entries expire after 2 seconds
def fx_rate(pair: str) -> float:
    print("  fetching", pair)
    return 1.08

fx_rate("EURUSD"); fx_rate("EURUSD")     # fetches once
time.sleep(2.1)
fx_rate("EURUSD")                        # expired, fetches again
# Each worker process has its OWN copy: with 4 gunicorn workers there are
# 4 caches that can hold different values until each one expires.

replace_subtopics.title: Cache-aside, TTLs and invalidation
replace_subtopics.body:
Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) is the most common pattern. On a read, the app checks the cache. On a hit it returns the copy. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache, and returns it. The cache only ever holds data someone asked for.

A TTL (time to live) makes each entry expire on its own after a set time. Choose it from the business: how stale may this value be? A product description can be an hour old; a stock level shown at checkout maybe a few seconds.

Invalidation means deleting or updating a cached entry when the source changes. The simplest reliable approach is to delete the key after a successful write so the next read reloads it. Other options are write-through (update the cache during the write) and versioned keys (change the key when the schema or logic changes, for example product:42:v2).

A cache has limited memory, so something must be removed when it is full. This is eviction. LRU (least recently used) throws out what nobody read for the longest time; LFU (least frequently used) throws out what is read least often. In Redis, set maxmemory (for example 2gb) and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for a pure cache. The default policy, noeviction, makes writes fail when memory is full.

Cache 'not found' too. If many requests ask for a product that does not exist, each one misses the cache and hits the database. Negative caching stores a marker meaning 'none' with a short TTL, such as 30 seconds.

A stampede happens when a popular key expires and hundreds of requests rebuild it at the same time. The fix in the code is a single-flight lock: SET lock:key NX EX 10 succeeds for only one caller, which rebuilds; the others wait briefly and read the fresh value. Another fix is early refresh, rebuilding a hot key shortly before it expires.

Design keys carefully. Include the tenant id, the permission scope or user id when the value depends on who asks, and a version: t:{tenant}:{scope}:product:42:v4. A key without the tenant or user is how one customer's data gets shown to another.
replace_subtopics.example: An airline's fare search caches route prices for 5 minutes. When the revenue team changes a fare, the pricing service deletes the affected keys, so customers see the new price on their next search. When a developer changes the response format, they bump the key prefix from v3 to v4 so old entries are simply ignored and expire. During a flash sale, the airline's top route key expires and 800 searches arrive in the same second. With the NX lock, one request rebuilds the price and the others wait about 100 ms, so the pricing database sees one query instead of 800.

replace_subtopics.title: Caching LLM responses and prompts
replace_subtopics.body:
LLM calls are slow and billed per token, so they are good candidates for caching. There are two distinct kinds.

Response caching is your own cache: hash the full request (model, system prompt, messages, parameters) and store the answer. An identical request returns the stored answer instantly and for free. It helps when the same questions repeat, such as classifying the same product titles again. Semantic caching goes further and matches similar questions using embeddings, which saves more but can return a wrong answer for a question that only looks similar, so use it carefully.

Prompt caching is a provider feature. Many requests share a long identical start: a big system prompt, tool definitions, or a long document. The provider can store its processed form of that prefix for a short time, so later requests that start the same way are cheaper and faster, while the model still writes a fresh answer. With the Anthropic API you mark the end of the reusable prefix with cache_control, and the usage fields report tokens written to and read from the cache.

Without prompt caching, each question pays for all the contract tokens again. With the contract marked as a cacheable prefix, follow-up questions within the cache lifetime read it from the cache, which the usage fields confirm, and responses start sooner.
