replace_subtopics.title: Queues versus logs
replace_subtopics.body:
A message queue, such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ, is built for distributing work. Each message is delivered to one consumer. When the consumer finishes, it acknowledges (acks) or deletes the message and it is gone. If the consumer crashes, the message becomes visible again and another worker gets it.

A log, such as Apache Kafka, is built for streams of events. Messages are appended in order to partitions and kept for a set retention period. Many independent consumer groups can each read the whole stream at their own pace, and they can go back and replay old events.

Use a queue for 'please do this task'. Use a log for 'this happened', when several systems need to react to the same events or you need replay. Redis can also act as a simple broker for Celery or RQ, which is common for small and medium projects.

Standard SQS queues deliver at least once and only roughly in order. When order matters for one key, such as all events for one bank account, use a FIFO queue. Each message gets a message group id (the account number). Messages in the same group are delivered strictly in order, one at a time, while different groups are processed in parallel. FIFO queues also drop duplicates: if the same message deduplication id (for example the event id) is sent again within five minutes, the second copy is ignored. That protects against a producer that retries a send. It does not make the whole system exactly once, because a worker can still crash after doing the work and before deleting the message, so tasks must still be idempotent.

Other clouds have equivalents: Google Cloud Pub/Sub (with ordering keys) and Azure Service Bus (with sessions for per-key order and dead-lettering built in). Kafka gives per-key order by sending all messages with the same key to the same partition.
replace_subtopics.example: An online retailer uses both. Kafka carries the 'order placed' event stream, which the warehouse, the email service and the analytics pipeline each consume independently. SQS holds 'generate invoice PDF' tasks, where each task is handled by whichever worker is free. SQS may deliver a task more than once, so the invoice task is idempotent and the effect happens once. A bank's account events go into a FIFO queue with the account number as the group id, so 'opened' is always processed before 'deposit' for that account, while thousands of other accounts are processed in parallel.

replace_subtopics.title: Workers with Celery and RQ
replace_subtopics.body:
A worker is a long-running process that pulls tasks from a queue and runs them. In Python, Celery is the most widely used framework: you decorate a function as a task, call task.delay(args) to enqueue it, and run worker processes that execute it. It works with Redis or RabbitMQ as the broker. RQ (Redis Queue) is a smaller, simpler alternative that uses only Redis.

Scale by running more workers, or more processes per worker. Keep the message small: pass an id, and let the worker load the data from the database or object storage. Big payloads in messages are slow and hit size limits (SQS raised its maximum to 1 MiB in 2025, and other brokers differ, so check the current limit).

Set a time limit on each task so a hung call cannot block a worker forever, and watch the queue length. A queue that keeps growing means workers are too few or too slow.

Some jobs run longer than the queue's visibility timeout, such as transcribing a long call. If the timeout passes while the worker is still busy, the message becomes visible again and a second worker starts the same job. You could set a very long timeout, but then a crashed job waits a long time before a retry. The better fix is a heartbeat: while working, the worker calls ChangeMessageVisibility every minute to push the timeout out a little further. If the worker dies, the beats stop and the message comes back quickly.

Plan for backpressure too. When producers add work faster than workers finish it, the queue grows without limit. Watch the depth, slow down or reject new work (return 429 or 'try later') when it passes a limit, and scale workers on queue depth. Big batch jobs can also starve small urgent ones sitting behind them in the same queue. Use separate queues for priorities, for example 'interactive' and 'bulk', each with its own workers (in Celery, route tasks with task_routes and start workers with -Q interactive).
replace_subtopics.example: A marketing agency client uploads 12,000 product descriptions to be rewritten by an LLM. The API creates one task per product with only the product id. Twenty Celery worker processes consume them. Queue depth starts at 12,000 and falls steadily; a dashboard of queue depth and tasks per minute shows the job will finish in about 40 minutes. The agency's 12,000-product batch goes to a 'bulk' queue with 16 workers, while single rewrites a user clicks in the app go to an 'interactive' queue with 4 dedicated workers, so a user never waits behind the batch.

replace_subtopics.title: Retries, dead letters and idempotency
replace_subtopics.body:
Classify failures. Transient errors (timeouts, 429 rate limits, 503s) are worth retrying. Permanent errors (bad input, a 400 or 404, a bug) will fail again, so record them and stop. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter: wait roughly 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds with some randomness, up to a maximum number of attempts.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where messages go after they have failed too many times. In SQS you set a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount on the source queue. The DLQ keeps the failed message for inspection and replay, and an alert on its size tells someone to look.

Most queues deliver at least once, so a message can arrive twice, for example when a worker finishes but crashes before acknowledging. So every task must be idempotent: running it twice has the same effect as running it once. Common techniques are an idempotency key with a unique constraint, checking the job's status before acting, and upserts instead of inserts.

In Celery, three settings make at-least-once processing safe. task_acks_late=True acknowledges a task only after it finishes, so a crash in the middle means the task is delivered again (the default acks it when received, and the task is lost). worker_prefetch_multiplier=1 stops each process from reserving a pile of tasks it cannot start yet. On the task itself, autoretry_for lists the transient exceptions to retry, retry_backoff and retry_jitter give exponential backoff with randomness, and max_retries caps the attempts. After that the task fails and your code or monitoring records it as a dead letter.

There is one more gap. Suppose the API saves an order in the database, then crashes just before sending the 'make invoice' message. The order exists but no invoice is ever made. Sending first and saving second has the opposite problem. The transactional outbox pattern closes the gap: in the same database transaction as the order, insert a row into an outbox table. A small relay process reads unsent outbox rows, publishes them and marks them sent. Either both rows are saved or neither is. The relay may publish a row twice after a crash, which is fine because consumers are idempotent.
replace_subtopics.example: A payments client sends payout jobs. Worker A pays invoice 7731, then its machine restarts before deleting the message. Worker B receives the same message. Because the payout table has a unique constraint on invoice_id and the task uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, the second attempt does nothing and the supplier is paid once. An online shop found 30 orders a month with no invoice after deploys restarted the API mid-request. Moving to an outbox table meant every committed order produced its invoice message, sometimes twice, which the idempotent invoice task ignored.
checklist: Separate transient errors (retry) from permanent ones (fail fast)
Exponential backoff with jitter, and a maximum attempts count
Visibility timeout or ack deadline longer than the task takes
Dead-letter queue configured, with an alert on its depth
Idempotency key or unique constraint on every side effect
A tested way to replay messages from the DLQ
Celery: task_acks_late=True and worker_prefetch_multiplier=1
Use an outbox table when a DB write must always produce a message

    pass

          autoretry_for=(TransientError,),   # retry only transient errors

# --- Transactional outbox ---
# Transactional outbox: save the row and the "to publish" row in ONE transaction
import json, sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total REAL);
CREATE TABLE outbox(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, topic TEXT,
                    payload TEXT, sent INTEGER DEFAULT 0);
""")

def place_order(order_id: int, total: float):
    with db:                                   # one transaction: both or neither
        db.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?)", (order_id, total))
        db.execute("INSERT INTO outbox(topic, payload) VALUES (?, ?)",
                   ("make_invoice", json.dumps({"order_id": order_id})))

def relay(send):                               # a small loop run every second
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, topic, payload FROM outbox WHERE sent = 0 ORDER BY id").fetchall()
    for row_id, topic, payload in rows:
        send(topic, payload)                   # publish (may repeat after a crash,
        with db:                               #  so consumers stay idempotent)
            db.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent = 1 WHERE id = ?", (row_id,))

place_order(55120, 99.0)
relay(lambda topic, payload: print("published", topic, payload))
relay(lambda topic, payload: print("published", topic, payload))   # nothing left
# published make_invoice {"order_id": 55120}

replace_subtopics.title: Webhooks in and out
replace_subtopics.body:
A webhook is an HTTP POST that one system sends to another when something happens, so the receiver does not have to poll. You send them to tell customers a job is done, and you receive them from tools like Stripe, GitHub or a CRM.

When sending, include an event id and type, sign the body with an HMAC (a keyed hash using a secret shared with the receiver), and retry with backoff if the receiver fails. Treat the send itself as a queued job.

When receiving, verify the signature before trusting anything, reply 2xx quickly, and put the real work on your own queue. Senders retry too, so deduplicate on the event id.

A valid signature is not enough on its own. An attacker who captures one real webhook could send it again later, and the signature would still match. To stop such replays, the sender puts a timestamp in the header and signs the timestamp together with the body, as Stripe does with t=...,v1=.... The receiver recomputes the signature and rejects the request if the timestamp is more than about five minutes old. Deduplicating on the event id catches replays inside that window.

Signing secrets should be rotated, for example yearly or after a person with access leaves. To rotate without downtime, the receiver accepts both the old and the new secret for a short overlap, the sender switches to the new one, and then the old one is removed.
replace_subtopics.example: A CRM sends your app a webhook every time a deal closes. Your endpoint checks the X-Signature header, stores the event id, enqueues a 'sync deal' task and returns 200 in 30 ms. When the CRM retries the same event after a network blip, the stored event id makes your endpoint skip it. The CRM integration verifies t and v1, rejects anything older than 300 seconds, and during a secret rotation accepts both secrets for 24 hours.

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException

async def crm_webhook(request: Request):
    body = await request.body()                       # raw bytes, before parsing
    expected = hmac.new(SECRET, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, request.headers.get("X-Signature", "")):
        raise HTTPException(401, "bad signature")
    event = await request.json()
    if seen_events.add_if_new(event["id"]):          # dedupe retries
        sync_deal.delay(event["data"]["deal_id"])    # real work on the queue
    return {"ok": True}                               # answer fast

# --- Replay protection and secret rotation ---
# Replay protection: sign "timestamp.body", reject old timestamps,
# and accept the old AND new secret while you rotate.
import hmac, hashlib, time

def sign(secret: bytes, body: bytes, ts: int) -> str:
    mac = hmac.new(secret, f"{ts}.".encode() + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return f"t={ts},v1={mac}"                       # Stripe-style header value

def verify(header: str, body: bytes, secrets: list[bytes], tolerance=300) -> bool:
    parts = dict(p.split("=", 1) for p in header.split(","))
    ts = int(parts["t"])
    if abs(time.time() - ts) > tolerance:            # older than 5 minutes: replay
        return False
    for s in secrets:                                # current and previous secret
        good = hmac.new(s, f"{ts}.".encode() + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        if hmac.compare_digest(good, parts["v1"]):
            return True
    return False

OLD, NEW = b"whsec_old", b"whsec_new"
body = b'{"id": "evt_91", "type": "deal.closed"}'
now = int(time.time())
print(verify(sign(NEW, body, now), body, [NEW, OLD]))          # True
print(verify(sign(OLD, body, now), body, [NEW, OLD]))          # True, during rotation
print(verify(sign(NEW, body, now - 3600), body, [NEW, OLD]))   # False, replayed
print(verify(sign(NEW, b'{"id": "evt_92"}', now), body, [NEW])) # False, body changed

replace_subtopics.title: Scheduling long LLM jobs
replace_subtopics.body:
LLM jobs add their own constraints: per-minute rate limits on requests and tokens, calls that take seconds to minutes, and occasional overload errors. Control concurrency so the total stays under your rate limits, for example a fixed number of worker processes or a token bucket shared through Redis.

For work that repeats on a timetable, use a scheduler: cron, Celery beat, or a cloud scheduler such as EventBridge Scheduler or Cloud Scheduler. The scheduler should only enqueue jobs; workers do the work, so a slow run never overlaps the next one's trigger in the same process.

When results are not needed right away, a provider batch API can be a good fit. For example, the Anthropic Message Batches API accepts many requests at once, processes them asynchronously at a lower price, and lets you fetch the results when the batch ends. Track each item with a custom id so you can match results to your records and retry just the failures.

Chaining Celery tasks works for two or three steps. Real pipelines often have more: ingest a file, split it, embed the chunks, wait for a human review that may take days, then notify the customer. Each step can fail, and you need to know where every item is. Durable workflow engines are the step up. AWS Step Functions describes the steps as a state machine with retries and waits built in. Temporal lets you write the workflow as ordinary code whose progress is saved after each step, so it continues after crashes and restarts. On Azure, Durable Functions or Logic Apps play the same role, and on Google Cloud, Workflows. Reach for one when a job has many steps, long waits or human approval.

The queue itself also has cloud equivalents: SQS on AWS, Google Cloud Pub/Sub on Google Cloud and Azure Service Bus on Azure. The ideas in this lesson (acks, retries, dead letters, idempotency) carry over to all of them.
replace_subtopics.example: A healthcare client (with a BAA in place) wants every new discharge summary from the day coded into categories by 6 a.m. At 1 a.m. a scheduled task collects the day's 3,000 summaries and submits them as one message batch, each with custom_id set to the document id. A second scheduled task polls the batch, writes results to the database, and re-queues the few errored items as normal tasks. A contract-review pipeline (ingest, extract clauses, LLM risk scoring, lawyer approval, email) moves from chained Celery tasks to a Temporal workflow. When a lawyer takes three days to approve, the workflow simply waits, and a worker restart in the middle loses nothing.

add_subtopics.title: Backups and disaster recovery
add_subtopics.body:
Every customer security review asks: what happens if the database is lost or the region goes down? Two numbers frame the answer. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data, measured in time, you may lose: an RPO of 15 minutes means that after a disaster you can restore to at most 15 minutes before it. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you may be down before service is back. Ask the customer for both; they drive cost.

Different setups protect against different disasters. A Multi-AZ database keeps a standby copy in a second data center in the same region and fails over in a minute or two. It protects against a machine or data center failure, but not against a mistake: a bad DELETE is copied to the standby at once. For mistakes you need backups. Managed databases take daily snapshots and also keep the change log, which allows point-in-time restore to any second in the retention window, for example 7 to 35 days. For a whole-region outage you need a copy in a second region, such as a cross-region replica or copied backups, plus a way to start the app there.

Remember the other stores: object storage (turn on versioning), the vector index (can you rebuild it from documents, and how long does that take?), secrets and configuration.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Run a restore drill at least every quarter: restore into a fresh environment, check the data, and time it. That measured time is your real RTO. In the customer's design document, the DR section should state the RPO and RTO targets, what is backed up and where, retention, who can trigger a failover, and the date and result of the last drill.
add_subtopics.example: A logistics customer asks for RPO 15 minutes and RTO 1 hour. Nightly snapshots alone would lose up to a day, so the FDE proposes Multi-AZ Postgres with point-in-time restore, a cross-region replica, and a monthly drill. The first drill takes 48 minutes, including rebuilding the vector index from stored embeddings, and that number goes into the DR section.

    ("Snapshot + point-in-time restore",         5,  90),

target_rpo, target_rto = 15, 60        # what the customer asked for, in minutes
for name, rpo, rto in setups:

replace_subtopics.title: Clients, load balancers, stateless servers
replace_subtopics.body:
A request starts at a client: a browser, a mobile app or another program. It travels over the internet to a public address. That address usually belongs to a load balancer, a component whose only job is to forward each request to one of several app servers and to stop sending traffic to any server that fails its health check (a small 'are you alive?' request it sends every few seconds).

An app server runs your code, for example a FastAPI service. It is stateless when it keeps nothing important in its own memory or disk between requests. Logged-in sessions go in a shared store such as Redis, uploaded files go in object storage such as S3, and records go in the database.

Stateless servers are interchangeable. You can run three, then ten, and the load balancer can send any request to any of them. If one crashes, nothing is lost.

In front of the app servers there is often an API gateway, such as AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee or an Nginx layer. It checks API keys or tokens, routes paths to the right service, and enforces rate limits so one noisy tenant cannot take down everyone. The usual rate-limit method is a token bucket per user or tenant: the bucket holds, say, 10 tokens and refills at 5 per second; each request takes one, and an empty bucket means HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

Large files should not flow through the app servers at all. Static files go through a CDN. For uploads, the app hands the browser a pre-signed URL: a link to object storage (such as S3) that allows one action on one key for a few minutes. The browser uploads the 200 MB file straight to storage, and only a small 'upload finished' message reaches the app, which then queues processing.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims portal runs on one server that stores login sessions in memory. When the team adds a second server behind a load balancer, users get logged out at random, because half their requests land on the server that never saw them log in. Moving sessions into Redis makes both servers stateless and the problem disappears. A contracts platform let users upload 500 MB scans through its FastAPI servers, which ran out of memory at month-end. Switching to pre-signed S3 uploads and adding a per-tenant limit of 20 requests per second at the gateway ended both the crashes and one tenant's script flooding the API.

# FastAPI app server that stays stateless.
# Session data lives in Redis, shared by every server copy.
import os, redis
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header

app = FastAPI()
store = redis.Redis.from_url(os.environ["REDIS_URL"])  # shared, not local memory

@app.get("/health")                 # the load balancer calls this every few seconds
def health():
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/me")
def me(session_id: str = Header(...)):
    user = store.get(f"session:{session_id}")   # works on ANY server copy
    return {"user": user.decode() if user else None}

# --- Rate limiting and pre-signed uploads ---
# Token bucket rate limit per tenant (what an API gateway does for you)
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_s: float, burst: int):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate_per_s, burst
        self.tokens, self.last = float(burst), time.monotonic()

    def allow(self) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False                      # caller returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests

buckets = {}                              # one bucket per tenant (in Redis when shared)
def check(tenant: str) -> bool:
    b = buckets.setdefault(tenant, TokenBucket(rate_per_s=5, burst=10))
    return b.allow()

print(sum(check("brightfield") for _ in range(25)), "of 25 instant requests allowed")
# 10 of 25 instant requests allowed   (the burst); then 5 more per second

# Large uploads skip the app servers: hand the browser a pre-signed URL

        Params={"Bucket": "brightfield-uploads", "Key": "tenant-7/contract-001.pdf"},
        ExpiresIn=900)                    # valid for 15 minutes, for this one key
print(url.split("?")[0])

replace_subtopics.title: Scaling, availability and CAP
replace_subtopics.body:
Vertical scaling means moving to a bigger machine with more CPU and memory. It needs no code changes, but it has a ceiling and the machine is still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines. It has no hard ceiling, but only works cleanly for stateless parts; databases are much harder to spread across machines.

Availability is the percentage of time a system answers correctly. 99.9 percent allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month; 99.99 percent allows about 4 minutes. You raise availability by removing single points of failure: two or more app servers, a database replica ready to take over, and servers in more than one availability zone (separate data centers in the same cloud region).

The CAP theorem says that when the network between parts of a distributed data store breaks (a partition), the store must choose: keep answering with data that might be out of date (favoring availability), or refuse some requests until it can be sure the data is current (favoring consistency). A bank balance usually favors consistency. A product review count can favor availability.

When a dependency such as an LLM API gets slow or fails, the danger is that every request waits for its timeout, all server threads fill up, and your whole app goes down with it. A circuit breaker prevents this. It counts failures; after too many in a row it 'opens' and fails fast for a while without calling the dependency. After a pause it lets one trial call through, and if that works it closes again. A bulkhead is a separate, limited pool for each dependency (for example at most 20 concurrent LLM calls), so one slow dependency cannot use up every worker. Combine both with graceful degradation: when the LLM is unavailable, show search results only, or a cached answer, instead of an error page.

When one database machine cannot hold all the data or writes, you shard (partition) it: split rows across several databases by a key such as tenant_id, so each shard holds some tenants. Pick a key that spreads load evenly and keeps a request on one shard. Sharding adds a lot of complexity, so use read replicas, caching and a bigger machine first.

Consistency is a choice per feature. Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write. Eventual consistency means replicas catch up after a short delay. A useful middle ground is read-your-writes: after a user saves something, send that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds, so they always see their own change while other reads use replicas.
replace_subtopics.example: A travel booking site runs one large database server. At 99.9 percent availability it is allowed about 43 minutes of downtime a month, and a single 2 hour hardware failure blows the budget. Adding a standby replica in a second availability zone that takes over automatically turns that 2 hour outage into a failover of a minute or two, while the app servers, being stateless, simply scale out from two to six copies during a holiday sale. When the LLM provider has a 20-minute outage, the document Q&A app's circuit breaker opens after three timeouts. Users see 'The assistant is unavailable; here are the most relevant documents' within 200 ms, instead of waiting 30 seconds for an error, and the rest of the portal keeps working.

# --- Circuit breaker with a degraded fallback ---
# Circuit breaker with graceful degradation
import time

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, max_failures=3, reset_after=30.0):
        self.max_failures, self.reset_after = max_failures, reset_after
        self.failures, self.opened_at = 0, None

    def call(self, fn, fallback):
        if self.opened_at is not None:
            if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at < self.reset_after:
                return fallback()                  # OPEN: do not even try
            self.opened_at = None                  # HALF-OPEN: allow one trial call
        try:
            result = fn()
            self.failures = 0                      # success closes the breaker
            return result
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.max_failures:
                self.opened_at = time.monotonic()  # trip: stop calling for a while
            return fallback()

def llm_answer():                    # pretend the LLM provider is down
    raise TimeoutError("LLM timed out after 10 s")

def search_only():                   # degraded mode: still useful
    return "LLM unavailable, here are the top 3 matching documents"

breaker = CircuitBreaker(max_failures=3, reset_after=30)
for i in range(5):
    print(i, breaker.call(llm_answer, search_only)[:15], "open" if breaker.opened_at else "closed")
# 0 LLM unavailable closed
# 1 LLM unavailable closed
# 2 LLM unavailable open      <- third failure trips the breaker
# 3 LLM unavailable open      <- answered at once, no 10 s wait
# 4 LLM unavailable open

replace_subtopics.title: Running a system design interview
replace_subtopics.body:
A system design interview is usually 45 to 60 minutes with an open prompt such as 'design a URL shortener' or 'design a support chatbot for an airline'. The interviewer is watching how you think: whether you ask the right questions, make sensible estimates, and explain trade-offs. There is no single correct answer.

Use a fixed order so you do not freeze. Spend the first 5 to 10 minutes on requirements and numbers. Then draw the simplest design that works end to end. Then go deep on one or two parts the interviewer cares about, and finish with failure modes, monitoring and what you would do next.

For FDE roles, bring the customer into it. Say who the users are, what data they are allowed to see, how you would roll it out to a pilot group first, and how you would measure whether it is working. That practical angle is what separates FDE candidates from pure backend candidates.

Two questions come up in almost every design. First, monolith or microservices? The safe default is a modular monolith: one deployable app with clear internal modules (ingest, search, chat, admin) that talk through defined interfaces. It is simpler to build, test and run. Split a module into its own service only for a clear reason, such as very different scaling needs (GPU workers), a separate team, or a separate security boundary.

Second, does the LLM deserve its own box? Add an LLM gateway when you use several models or providers, need a fallback provider when one fails, want per-tenant token quotas and cost tracking, or must log and redact prompts centrally. For a single model in a small pilot, a thin client module inside the app is enough.
replace_subtopics.example: Prompt: 'Design a chatbot that answers questions about a hospital's internal procedures.' A strong opening: 'Who are the users, clinicians or all staff? Roughly how many? Must answers cite the procedure document? Is any patient data involved, and where must the data stay? What response time is acceptable on a ward tablet?' Only after the answers does the candidate draw the first box. Asked to design an airline support chatbot, a candidate draws one FastAPI app with modules plus separate ingestion workers, then adds an LLM gateway box once the interviewer mentions three business units with separate budgets and a need for a backup provider.
checklist: Restate the problem and name the users
Ask for scale: users, requests per second, data size, growth
Ask about constraints: latency, security, data location, budget
Write down the core features and what is out of scope
Do a quick back-of-envelope estimate out loud
Draw the simple end-to-end design first
Go deep on the hardest part (retrieval, permissions, data model)
Cover failures: what breaks, how you detect it, how you recover
Mention monitoring, cost and a phased rollout
Summarize trade-offs and what you would do with more time

add_glossary: RPO
Recovery point objective: the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose in a disaster.
RTO
Recovery time objective: the longest the service may be down before it is restored.
Point-in-time restore
Restoring a database to any moment within a retention window, using snapshots plus the change log.
Restore drill
A scheduled practice restore that proves backups work and measures the real RTO.
Circuit breaker
A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while and fails fast instead.
Bulkhead
A separate, limited resource pool per dependency so one failure cannot use up everything.
Graceful degradation
Offering a reduced but useful service when a part of the system fails.
Sharding
Splitting a database's rows across several databases by a key such as tenant id.
Read-your-writes
A consistency guarantee that a user always sees their own recent changes.
API gateway
A front door service that authenticates, routes and rate-limits API requests.

A rate-limit method where requests spend tokens that refill at a fixed rate.

add_subtopics.title: WebSockets and real-time channels
add_subtopics.body:
Plain HTTP is request and reply: the client asks, the server answers, done. Some features need the server to push data as it happens, or both sides to talk at once. There are three common ways.

Long polling: the client sends a request and the server holds it open until there is news or about 30 seconds pass, then the client asks again. It works everywhere but is clumsy. Server-Sent Events (SSE): one HTTP response that stays open while the server writes events into it, one way only, from server to client. It is the usual choice for streaming LLM tokens, it reconnects automatically in browsers, and it is taught in the fastapi lesson. WebSockets: the client upgrades an HTTP connection into a two-way channel that stays open, and both sides send messages whenever they like. You need them for voice agents streaming audio both ways, live agent-assist during a call, collaborative editing and multiplayer features.

WebSockets bring work of their own. Authenticate when the connection opens, because browsers cannot add an Authorization header to a WebSocket request: pass a short-lived token in the URL or in the first message, and close the connection if it is wrong. Send heartbeats (a ping every 20 to 30 seconds) so dead connections are noticed and proxies do not close idle ones. Expect disconnects: the client must reconnect with backoff and resume, for example by sending the last message id it received. Load balancers must allow long-lived connections, and because each connection sticks to one server, scaling needs a shared channel such as Redis pub/sub to reach users on other servers.
add_subtopics.example: A contact centre wants live suggestions while an agent is on a call. The call transcript streams to the server and suggestions stream back in the same moment, so the FDE uses a WebSocket authenticated with a 60-second token, with a ping every 25 seconds. The separate 'summarise this call' button just streams its answer over SSE.

# WebSocket endpoint: authenticate on connect, then talk both ways
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect, status

app = FastAPI()
VALID = {"tok-123": "agent-7"}               # use real token checks in production

@app.websocket("/ws/assist")
async def assist(ws: WebSocket):
    user = VALID.get(ws.query_params.get("token", ""))   # browsers cannot set
    if user is None:                                       # auth headers here
        await ws.close(code=status.WS_1008_POLICY_VIOLATION)
        return
    await ws.accept()
    try:
        while True:
            msg = await ws.receive_json()
            if msg["type"] == "ping":                      # app-level heartbeat
                await ws.send_json({"type": "pong"})
            elif msg["type"] == "transcript":              # live call text arrives
                await ws.send_json({"type": "suggestion",
                                    "text": f"Suggest refund policy for: {msg['text']}"})
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        pass                                               # client left; clean up

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
    with TestClient(app).websocket_connect("/ws/assist?token=tok-123") as ws:
        ws.send_json({"type": "ping"}); print(ws.receive_json())
        ws.send_json({"type": "transcript", "text": "my parcel is late"})
        print(ws.receive_json())
    # {'type': 'pong'}
    # {'type': 'suggestion', 'text': 'Suggest refund policy for: my parcel is late'}

replace_subtopics.title: REST: resources, verbs, status codes
replace_subtopics.body:
REST (representational state transfer) organizes an API around resources, which are the nouns of the system: orders, customers, invoices. Each resource has a URL, such as /orders/42. You act on it with HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes. The HTTP basics themselves are covered in the http concept.

The server answers with a status code that tells you what happened. 200 means OK, 201 means created, 400 means your request was malformed, 401 means you are not logged in, 404 means the thing does not exist, 429 means slow down, and 5xx means the server failed.

REST is popular because every language, tool and developer already understands it. Its weak spot is that the server decides the response shape, so a screen may need several calls to gather everything, or receive far more data than it uses.

A few conventions make a REST API safe to use in production. POST is not idempotent: if the network fails after the server created a refund, a retry creates a second one. Many APIs (Stripe is the best known) accept an Idempotency-Key header on POST. The client makes a unique key per operation and sends the same key on every retry; the server stores the first result for that key and returns it again instead of acting twice.

Errors should have a standard body. RFC 9457 defines application/problem+json with the fields type, title, status, detail and instance, so every client can read any error the same way. Rate limits are announced in headers: 429 responses carry Retry-After, and many APIs send RateLimit or X-RateLimit-Remaining headers so clients can slow down before hitting the limit. Lists are paginated with a limit and a cursor or page; the http lesson covers pagination in detail.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer called Lindqvist Outdoor exposes GET /orders?status=open&limit=50. Your script receives 50 orders as JSON. To show each order's customer name, it then calls GET /customers/{id} for each order, making 51 requests in total. That extra chatter is the problem GraphQL was designed to reduce. Lindqvist Outdoor's refund endpoint gets a timeout from its load balancer and the client retries. Because both calls carry the same Idempotency-Key, the customer gets one 15.00 refund, not two, and a bad amount returns a problem+json body the partner's code already knows how to read.

import requests

BASE = "https://api.example-retailer.com/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": "Bearer <token>"}

# GET a filtered list of resources
r = requests.get(f"{BASE}/orders", params={"status": "open", "limit": 50},
                 headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()                 # turns 4xx/5xx into an exception
orders = r.json()["data"]

# POST creates a new resource; expect 201 Created
new = requests.post(f"{BASE}/orders/{orders[0]['id']}/notes",
                    json={"text": "Customer called about delivery"},
                    headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
print(new.status_code)               # 201 on success

# Server side: Idempotency-Key on POST and RFC 9457 problem+json errors
import uuid
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

app = FastAPI()
seen: dict[str, dict] = {}                   # use a DB table with a TTL in production

def problem(status: int, title: str, detail: str, request: Request, **extra):
    return JSONResponse(status_code=status, media_type="application/problem+json",
        content={"type": "https://api.example-retailer.com/problems/" + title.lower().replace(" ", "-"),
                 "title": title, "status": status, "detail": detail,
                 "instance": str(request.url.path), **extra})

@app.post("/v1/refunds", status_code=201)
def create_refund(body: dict, request: Request, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    if idempotency_key in seen:              # a retry: return the first result
        return seen[idempotency_key]
    if body.get("amount_cents", 0) <= 0:
        return problem(422, "Invalid amount", "amount_cents must be positive", request)
    refund = {"id": "rf_" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:6], "amount_cents": body["amount_cents"]}
    seen[idempotency_key] = refund
    return refund

c = TestClient(app)

a = c.post("/v1/refunds", json={"amount_cents": 1500}, headers=h).json()
b = c.post("/v1/refunds", json={"amount_cents": 1500}, headers=h).json()   # retry
print(a == b)                                # True: one refund, not two
bad = c.post("/v1/refunds", json={"amount_cents": 0}, headers={"Idempotency-Key": "x1"})
print(bad.status_code, bad.headers["content-type"], bad.json()["title"])

replace_subtopics.title: GraphQL: the client chooses the shape
replace_subtopics.body:
GraphQL exposes a single endpoint, usually /graphql, and a schema that lists every type and field. The client sends a query naming exactly which fields it needs, including related objects, and the server returns JSON in that same shape.

This helps when many different clients (a mobile app, a web dashboard, a partner) need different slices of the same data. One request can replace several REST calls, and nobody downloads fields they do not use.

The costs are real. HTTP caching is harder because everything is a POST to one URL. A careless query can ask for deeply nested data and overload the server, so servers set depth and cost limits. On the server side, resolving each nested field naively causes many database queries, the N+1 problem, which is usually fixed with batching.

Queries read data; mutations change it. A mutation looks like a query that starts with the word mutation and names the change and the fields to return, such as mutation { addNote(orderId: 42, text: "Called") { id } }. GraphQL servers also support introspection: you can ask the schema itself which types and fields exist, which is how tools like GraphiQL offer autocomplete. Many teams turn introspection off in production so outsiders cannot map the whole API.

Persisted queries help both caching and safety. The client registers its queries ahead of time and later sends only a hash or id. The server runs only known queries, which blocks expensive surprise queries, and because the request is small it can be sent as a GET, so CDNs and browsers can cache the response.
replace_subtopics.example: The Lindqvist Outdoor mobile app shows open orders with the customer's first name and the item count. With GraphQL it sends one query asking for orders { id total customer { firstName } items { sku } }. The response is about 8 KB instead of the roughly 60 KB the REST calls returned, and it takes one round trip instead of 51. Lindqvist's mobile app adds a note with one mutation and uses persisted queries for its five screens, so the product list is served from the CDN as a GET and unknown queries are rejected.

replace_subtopics.title: gRPC and Protobuf for internal services
replace_subtopics.body:
gRPC is a framework for calling a function on another service as if it were local. You describe the service and its messages in a .proto file using Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), a compact binary format. A code generator then produces client and server code in many languages, so both sides agree on types at compile time.

gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which keeps one connection open and can stream many messages in both directions. Messages are smaller and faster to parse than JSON.

The trade-off is reach. Browsers cannot call gRPC directly without a proxy, you cannot read a binary message with your eyes, and customers' developers are less familiar with it. It shines between services that one team controls.

Protobuf can evolve safely if you follow a few rules. Never change or reuse a field number, because old clients identify fields only by number. You may add new fields with new numbers; old clients simply ignore them. When you delete a field, mark its number and name as reserved so nobody reuses them by accident. Do not change a field's type.

Every gRPC call should have a deadline, the time after which the caller gives up (in Python, the timeout argument). Deadlines pass along a chain of services, so work stops everywhere once the caller no longer waits. Instead of HTTP codes, gRPC has its own status codes, such as OK, INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, UNAVAILABLE (usually safe to retry) and PERMISSION_DENIED. To poke at a gRPC service by hand, use grpcurl, the curl of gRPC.
replace_subtopics.example: A freight company runs a pricing service called by its booking service about 3,000 times per second. Moving that call from JSON over REST to gRPC cut the payload size and gave both teams a shared contract file, so a renamed field became a build error instead of a production bug. The freight team removes the old weight_lbs field. They reserve its number 4 and name, add weight_kg as field 5, and set a 300 ms deadline on every Quote call; slow calls now fail with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED instead of piling up.

replace_subtopics.title: Polling versus webhooks
replace_subtopics.body:
Polling means your code asks the other system on a timer: 'any new orders since 10:05?'. It is simple and works with any API, but most calls return nothing, and you learn about changes only at the next poll.

A webhook is an HTTP POST the other system sends to a URL you give it whenever an event happens, such as order.paid. You get the news within seconds and make no wasted calls. In exchange you must run a public endpoint, verify that each call really came from the sender (usually an HMAC signature header computed with a shared secret), reply quickly with a 2xx code, and handle duplicates and out-of-order events, because senders retry.

A common robust pattern is both: webhooks for speed, plus a slow reconciliation poll that catches anything missed during an outage.

One more style you will meet is JSON-RPC 2.0. Instead of resources and verbs, every call is a small JSON object naming a method and its params, with an id to match the reply: {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}. It is simple and works over HTTP, WebSockets or plain standard input and output. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), which connects AI apps to tools and data, is built on JSON-RPC 2.0, so you will read these messages when debugging an MCP server; see the mcp lesson.
replace_subtopics.example: A carrier offers a shipment status API and webhooks. Polling 4,000 open shipments every 5 minutes would be 48,000 calls an hour. With webhooks the carrier sends about 900 events an hour, and a nightly poll of shipments not updated in 24 hours catches the rare missed event. While debugging a customer's MCP server, the FDE reads the raw JSON-RPC log: a tools/call request with id 7, and a reply with id 7 carrying an error object, which shows the server rejected a missing argument.

import hmac, hashlib
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()
SECRET = b"shared-webhook-secret"          # from a secret store in real code

@app.post("/webhooks/carrier")
async def carrier_hook(request: Request):
    raw = await request.body()
    sent = request.headers.get("X-Signature", "")
    expected = hmac.new(SECRET, raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sent, expected):   # reject forged calls
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    event = await request.json()
    enqueue(event)            # do slow work later; reply fast
    return {"ok": True}       # 200 tells the sender not to retry

# JSON-RPC 2.0 (used by MCP): request and reply matched by id
# -> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_order", "arguments": {"id": 42}}}
# <- {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Order 42: shipped"}]}}

replace_subtopics.title: Versioning and OpenAPI specs
replace_subtopics.body:
An OpenAPI specification is a YAML or JSON document that describes a REST API: every path, verb, parameter, request body, response and error. Tools read it to generate documentation pages, client libraries, mock servers and tests. FastAPI generates one for you automatically at /openapi.json.

As an FDE, the spec is often the fastest way to understand a customer's API. Load it into a viewer, find the endpoints you need, and generate a typed client instead of hand-writing requests.

APIs change, and changes are either additive or breaking. Adding an optional field or a new endpoint is additive and safe. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or making an optional field required is breaking. Breaking changes need a new version, often in the path (/v2/orders) or a header, running beside the old one until clients have moved.

You rarely write a client for a large API by hand. Generate a typed client from the spec. For Python, openapi-python-client produces a package with a function and a data class per endpoint; openapi-generator produces clients in dozens of languages. When the customer updates the spec, you regenerate, and type checks show what changed. Note the version: FastAPI now produces OpenAPI 3.1, while some older tools only read 3.0, so check that your generator supports the spec's version.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer wants to split 'name' into 'first_name' and 'last_name' on its claims API. Changing /v1 would break three partner integrations. Instead it adds the new fields to /v1 alongside 'name' (additive), launches /v2 without 'name', and sets a sunset date for /v1 twelve months out, tracking which partners still call it. The insurer publishes its /v2 spec. The FDE runs openapi-python-client on it and gets a claims_api package; a type checker immediately flags the three places the integration still reads 'name'.

openapi: 3.0.3

  title: Claims API
  version: 2.0.0
paths:
  /v2/claims/{claimId}:
    get:
      summary: Get one claim
      parameters:
        - name: claimId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: {type: string}
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The claim
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [id, status]
                properties:
                  id: {type: string}
                  status: {type: string, enum: [open, approved, rejected]}
                  first_name: {type: string}
        "404": {description: Claim not found}

# Generate a typed Python client from the spec:
#   pip install openapi-python-client
#   openapi-python-client generate --url https://api.example-insurer.com/openapi.json
# Or any language:

replace_subtopics.title: Key-value stores: Redis and DynamoDB
replace_subtopics.body:
A key-value store does one thing very well: given a key, return or store its value. Redis keeps data in memory, so reads take well under a millisecond, and it offers extras like expiry times, counters and sorted sets. It is widely used for caches (see the caching concept), sessions and rate limiting.

Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database. Each table has a partition key, and optionally a sort key. Items with the same partition key are stored together, and you can query them by sort key range. DynamoDB scales very large, but you must design the keys around your queries in advance, because queries that do not use the key need a slow scan or a secondary index.

The common mistake is a hot partition: a key that most traffic shares, such as today's date, so one partition takes all the load.

Redis in practice. Redis values are not just strings. A counter with INCR is atomic, so two servers can add to it at once without losing a count. Pair it with an expiry to make a rate limiter: allow 5 calls per minute per customer. A sorted set keeps members ordered by a score, which makes a leaderboard: add scores, then read the top N. A hash stores several fields under one key, which suits a session with a user id and role. One caution: set the expiry when you create the counter (SET with EX and NX), because a crash between INCR and EXPIRE would leave a key that never expires.

DynamoDB in practice. If you need to query by something other than the table key, add a global secondary index (GSI), which is a second copy of the data with its own partition and sort key. Single-table design goes one step further: several entity types (customers, orders, scans) share one table, using generic key names like PK and SK and prefixes such as CUSTOMER#7 and ORDER#88, so one query fetches a customer and their orders together. It is fast and cheap but hard to change later, so write down every access pattern first.

Reads are eventually consistent by default, meaning a read right after a write may return the old value for a moment. Ask for ConsistentRead=True when you must see the latest write (it costs twice as much, and is not available on a GSI). For cost, on-demand capacity charges per request and suits spiky or unknown traffic. Provisioned capacity charges for a fixed read and write rate per second and is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic, especially with auto scaling.
replace_subtopics.example: A parcel tracking app stores scan events in DynamoDB with partition key parcel_id and sort key scanned_at. 'Show all scans for parcel P-88412, newest first' is one fast query. 'All parcels scanned in Leeds yesterday' is not supported by that key and would need a global secondary index. The parcel app now needs 'all parcels scanned at the Leeds depot', so the FDE adds a GSI with partition key depot and sort key scanned_at, and picks on-demand capacity because traffic spikes at Christmas. Separately, the same team uses Redis to stop one customer from calling its tracking API more than 100 times a minute, and shows a live leaderboard of the busiest depots.
replace_subtopics.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("parcel_scans")
# Table keys: partition key parcel_id, sort key scanned_at (ISO time string)

table.put_item(Item={
    "parcel_id": "P-88412",
    "scanned_at": "2026-03-02T09:14:00Z",
    "depot": "Leeds",
    "status": "out_for_delivery",
})

# Fast: uses the partition key and sorts by the sort key
resp = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("parcel_id").eq("P-88412"),
    ScanIndexForward=False,        # newest first
    Limit=10,
)
for item in resp["Items"]:
    print(item["scanned_at"], item["status"])

import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

# Rate limiter: 5 calls per 60 seconds per customer
def allow(customer_id, limit=5, window=60):
    key = f"rate:{customer_id}"
    r.set(key, 0, ex=window, nx=True)   # create with expiry only if missing
    return r.incr(key) <= limit          # INCR is atomic

print([allow("cust-7") for _ in range(7)])
# [True, True, True, True, True, False, False]

# Sorted set leaderboard
r.zadd("depot_scans", {"Leeds": 120, "York": 95, "Hull": 150})
r.zincrby("depot_scans", 30, "York")
print(r.zrevrange("depot_scans", 0, 2, withscores=True))
# [('Hull', 150.0), ('York', 125.0), ('Leeds', 120.0)]

# Hash: a session with several fields, expiring in 30 minutes
r.hset("session:abc", mapping={"user_id": "42", "role": "admin"})
r.expire("session:abc", 1800)
print(r.hget("session:abc", "role"))   # admin

# ---- DynamoDB: add a global secondary index and choose capacity ----
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

client = boto3.client("dynamodb")
client.create_table(
    TableName="parcel_scans",
    BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST",       # on-demand; use PROVISIONED for steady traffic
    AttributeDefinitions=[
        {"AttributeName": "parcel_id",  "AttributeType": "S"},
        {"AttributeName": "scanned_at", "AttributeType": "S"},
        {"AttributeName": "depot",      "AttributeType": "S"},
    ],
    KeySchema=[
        {"AttributeName": "parcel_id",  "KeyType": "HASH"},
        {"AttributeName": "scanned_at", "KeyType": "RANGE"},
    ],
    GlobalSecondaryIndexes=[{
        "IndexName": "by_depot",
        "KeySchema": [
            {"AttributeName": "depot",      "KeyType": "HASH"},
            {"AttributeName": "scanned_at", "KeyType": "RANGE"},
        ],
        "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "ALL"},
    }],
)

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("parcel_scans")

# Query the index: all scans at Leeds on or after 1 March
resp = table.query(
    IndexName="by_depot",
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("depot").eq("Leeds") & Key("scanned_at").gte("2026-03-01"),
)

# Strongly consistent read on the base table (not allowed on a GSI)
resp = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("parcel_id").eq("P-88412"),
    ConsistentRead=True,
)

# Single-table design keys: one table, several entity types
# PK="CUSTOMER#7"  SK="PROFILE"
# PK="CUSTOMER#7"  SK="ORDER#2026-03-02#88"   -> query PK, SK begins_with "ORDER#"

replace_subtopics.title: Document databases: MongoDB
replace_subtopics.body:
A document database stores records as documents, which are JSON-like objects that can contain nested lists and sub-objects. Documents live in collections, roughly like tables, but two documents in the same collection can have different fields.

The design rule is to store together what you read together. An order document can embed its line items and shipping address, so one read returns everything the order page needs. Things that are shared or grow without limit, like a product used by millions of orders, are usually referenced by id instead of embedded.

MongoDB supports indexes, rich queries and an aggregation pipeline, and multi-document transactions exist, but heavy cross-collection joins are less natural than in SQL.

Two more MongoDB tools are worth knowing. The aggregation pipeline is a list of stages, each transforming the documents from the previous stage: $match filters (put it first so an index can be used), $group totals by a key, and $lookup pulls in matching documents from another collection, like a left join. Second, although collections are flexible, you can still enforce rules with schema validation using $jsonSchema, so a document with a missing or wrongly typed field is rejected. This is a good middle path: flexibility where you need it, guard rails where the data must be right.
replace_subtopics.example: A furniture marketplace stores 40,000 products where a sofa has fabric and seat depth, and a lamp has wattage and bulb type. In MongoDB each product document carries only its own attributes, and the product page reads one document by id. The furniture marketplace wants 'revenue per product type in March'. An aggregation pipeline matches March orders, joins each order line to its product with $lookup, and groups by product type. It also adds validation so a product without a price or with a negative price cannot be saved.
replace_subtopics.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

db = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017")["shop"]

# Documents in one collection can have different fields
db.products.insert_many([
    {"sku": "SOFA-12", "type": "sofa", "price": 899,
     "attrs": {"fabric": "linen", "seat_depth_cm": 58}},
    {"sku": "LAMP-3", "type": "lamp", "price": 49,
     "attrs": {"watts": 8, "bulb": "E27"}},
])

db.products.create_index("sku", unique=True)

# Query by a nested field
for p in db.products.find({"type": "sofa", "attrs.fabric": "linen"}):
    print(p["sku"], p["price"])

from pymongo import MongoClient
from datetime import datetime

db = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017")["shop"]

# Schema validation: reject products that break the rules
db.create_collection("products_checked", validator={
    "$jsonSchema": {
        "bsonType": "object",
        "required": ["sku", "price"],
        "properties": {
            "sku":   {"bsonType": "string"},
            "price": {"bsonType": ["int", "double"], "minimum": 0},
        },
    }
})

# Aggregation pipeline: revenue per product type in March
pipeline = [
    {"$match": {"placed_at": {"$gte": datetime(2026, 3, 1), "$lt": datetime(2026, 4, 1)}}},
    {"$unwind": "$lines"},
    {"$lookup": {"from": "products", "localField": "lines.sku",
                 "foreignField": "sku", "as": "product"}},
    {"$unwind": "$product"},
    {"$group": {"_id": "$product.type",
               "revenue": {"$sum": {"$multiply": ["$lines.qty", "$lines.unit_price"]}}}},
    {"$sort": {"revenue": -1}},
]
for row in db.orders.aggregate(pipeline):
    print(row["_id"], row["revenue"])

replace_subtopics.title: A decision table for picking a database
replace_subtopics.body:
Start by writing down the five to ten most important queries and writes, with rough volumes and required response times. Then look for the store whose shape makes those operations simple. If a relational database handles them, stop there.

Next, weigh the operational side. Who will run backups, upgrades and monitoring? Is there a managed service in the customer's cloud? Does their security team already approve it? A technically ideal database that nobody can support is a poor choice.

It is normal to combine stores, a pattern called polyglot persistence: Postgres as the system of record, Redis for fast ephemeral data, and a search or vector index built from Postgres. Keep one clear source of truth and treat the others as copies you can rebuild.

Customers often name three more options, so know where they fit. A search engine such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch is built for full-text search with relevance ranking (BM25) and facets like 'filter by brand and price range'. It is usually a copy of data that lives elsewhere, not the system of record. A time-series database such as TimescaleDB (a Postgres extension) or InfluxDB stores timestamped measurements, compresses them well and answers questions like 'average per 5 minutes over the last day'. An analytical warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery) scans huge tables for reports and dashboards, but is slow and costly for single-row lookups and constant small writes. It is where finished data goes to be analysed, not where the app reads its orders.
replace_subtopics.example: A travel agency lists its needs: bookings with payments (transactions, reports), user sessions (millions of short reads), and 'find hotels like this one' (similarity). The answer: Postgres for bookings, Redis for sessions with a 30-minute expiry, and pgvector on the hotels table. The travel agency later adds a search box with typo tolerance and filters, plus hourly sensor data from its airport kiosks and a weekly board report. The answer grows to: OpenSearch fed from Postgres for search, TimescaleDB for kiosk readings, and a warehouse for the board report, each rebuilt from the Postgres source of truth.

checklist: Top queries and writes listed with volumes and latency targets
Checked whether Postgres (with JSONB or pgvector) already covers them
Transactions and reporting needs identified
Partition or primary key designed to avoid hot spots
Managed service available in the customer's cloud
Backup, restore and monitoring owner named
One system of record agreed; other stores rebuildable from it
If search, metrics or reporting are needed, decided which store is a rebuildable copy of the source of truth

replace_subtopics.title: Vector databases for AI search
replace_subtopics.body:
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text or an image (see the embeddings concept). Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together. A vector database stores these vectors and quickly finds the nearest ones to a query vector, using approximate indexes such as HNSW.

This powers semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (the rag concept). Options include dedicated services such as Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant and Milvus, and extensions like pgvector for Postgres.

For many enterprise projects, pgvector is a good first choice: the vectors sit next to the rows they describe, you can filter with normal SQL (for example by customer or permission), and there is no new system for the security team to review.

Three more points for real projects. First, hybrid search. Vectors find meaning ('ending the contract early') but can miss exact terms such as a clause number or product code, which classic keyword search (BM25 in a search engine, or full-text search in Postgres) finds easily. Hybrid search runs both and merges the two ranked lists, commonly with reciprocal rank fusion: each result scores 1 divided by (60 plus its rank) in each list, and the scores are added.

Second, HNSW is approximate, and it has a recall and speed knob. In pgvector it is hnsw.ef_search (default 40): a higher value examines more candidates, so it finds more of the true nearest rows but is slower. Index build settings m and ef_construction trade build time and memory for recall the same way.

Third, a pitfall with filters. The HNSW index returns about ef_search nearest candidates first, and the WHERE filter is applied afterwards. If the filter is restrictive (one team out of 500), most candidates are thrown away and you may get fewer than k rows, or none. Fixes: raise ef_search, use iterative index scans if your pgvector version supports them, or use partitions or partial indexes for large tenants. Always test with your real filters and check that you get k results.
replace_subtopics.example: A legal team has 300,000 contract clauses. Each clause row in Postgres gets a 1,024-number embedding. A question like 'termination for convenience with 30 days notice' is embedded, and the query returns the 5 closest clauses from contracts the user is allowed to see. The legal team's search for 'termination 30 days notice' is missing clause C-114, because its wording differs from the question. Adding keyword search and merging results with reciprocal rank fusion puts it in the top 5. Separately, a user from a small team gets only 2 results instead of 5, because 95 of the nearest 100 candidates belonged to other teams. Raising hnsw.ef_search to 200 fixes it.
replace_subtopics.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE clauses (
    id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    contract_id bigint NOT NULL,
    team_id     int    NOT NULL,       -- used for permission filtering
    body        text   NOT NULL,
    embedding   vector(1024)           -- produced by an embedding model
);

-- Approximate nearest-neighbour index using cosine distance
CREATE INDEX ON clauses USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- $1 is the query embedding, $2 the user's team
SELECT id, contract_id, left(body, 120) AS preview
FROM clauses
WHERE team_id = $2
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1              -- <=> is cosine distance
LIMIT 5;

-- Recall/speed knob: examine more candidates per query (default 40)
SET hnsw.ef_search = 200;

-- Hybrid search: keyword rank + vector rank merged with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)
-- $1 = query embedding, $2 = team id, $3 = the user's words
WITH keyword AS (
    SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(to_tsvector('english', body), q) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM clauses, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $3) q
    WHERE team_id = $2 AND to_tsvector('english', body) @@ q
    ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(to_tsvector('english', body), q) DESC
    LIMIT 20
),
semantic AS (
    SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rnk
    FROM clauses
    WHERE team_id = $2
    ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
    LIMIT 20
)
SELECT c.id, left(c.body, 100) AS preview,
       coalesce(1.0 / (60 + k.rnk), 0) + coalesce(1.0 / (60 + s.rnk), 0) AS score
FROM clauses c
LEFT JOIN keyword  k ON k.id = c.id
LEFT JOIN semantic s ON s.id = c.id
WHERE k.id IS NOT NULL OR s.id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- Pitfall check: a restrictive filter can return fewer than k rows
-- SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM clauses WHERE team_id = 42
--                       ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5) t;   -- expect 5

add_glossary: DynamoDB GSI
A global secondary index: a second copy of a table's data with a different partition and sort key, for other queries.
Single-table design
A DynamoDB pattern where several entity types share one table with generic PK and SK keys so one query returns related items.
Eventually consistent read
A read that may briefly return old data after a write; the DynamoDB default.
On-demand capacity
DynamoDB billing per request; suits spiky or unknown traffic. Provisioned capacity reserves a fixed rate and suits steady traffic.
Sorted set
A Redis structure that keeps members ordered by a score, used for leaderboards.
Aggregation pipeline
A MongoDB query made of stages such as $match, $group and $lookup that transform documents in turn.
$jsonSchema
MongoDB schema validation that rejects documents that break the declared field rules.
BM25
A standard formula for ranking documents by how well they match search words.
Hybrid search
Running keyword and vector search together and merging the ranked results.
Reciprocal rank fusion
A way to merge ranked lists by adding 1 / (60 + rank) for each list a result appears in.
ef_search
A pgvector HNSW setting: how many candidates a query examines; higher means better recall and slower queries.
Time-series database
A database built for timestamped measurements, with compression and rollups.
